full_text: Oct 10, 2026 8:00am PT ‘Squadron 42’ Release Nears as Cloud Imperium Opens Steam Wishlist By Mya Copeland Plus Icon Mya Copeland Latest ‘Star Wars: Galactic Racer’ Debuts on Amazon Luna Day and Date With Wide Release (Gaming News Roundup) 23 hours ago Ice-T on ‘Law & Order: SVU’s’ Longevity and Cultural Impact: ‘I’m on a Good Treadmill, and I Want to Stay on It’ 2 days ago Questlove Reflects on the Power of Vulnerability and Being a Trailblazer: ‘I Gotta Be the Change I Want to Be’ 3 days ago See All Cloud Imperium Games ’ “ Squadron 42 ” is now available to wishlist on Steam ahead of its planned Q2 2027 release. The single-player sci-fi adventure game is set in the year 2945, as the United Empire of Earth is threatened by outlaws and hostile aliens alike. Players enlist as a rookie in the UEE Navy and embark on a dangerous journey through the galactic war. Aboard a massive capital ship, players work alongside a dynamic crew to earn their rank. The CIG team has been developing “Star Citizen” simultaneously with “Squadron 42,” which follows a focused single-player narrative adventure rather than a multiplayer game style. Much of the technology and game systems utilized in “Star Citizen” is repurposed for “Squadron 42,” game designer and CIG founder Chris Roberts told Variety in May . Popular on Variety Its star-studded cast includes Mark Hamill, Gary Oldman, Gillian Anderson, Ben Mendelsohn, Henry Cavill, Andy Serkis, John Rhys-Davies, Jonathan Bailey, Mark Strong, Alix Wilton Reagan, Ben Mendelsohn, Damson Idris, Liam Cunningham, Jane Perry and more. “Squadron 42” is powered by StarEngine proprietary technology, which has been developed in-house at Cloud Imperium Games. The independent studio was co-founded in 2012 by game designer Roberts, the mind behind the ‘90s PC game “Wing Commander,” alongside wife Sandi Roberts. “Squadron 42” is slated for release in Q2 2027. Players can now wishlist the game on Steam. title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Breakout Portia Doubleday on Playing ‘White Girl Wasted’ Conspiracy Theorist: ‘I Knew People Who Were Radicalized’
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 8:00am PT ‘The Social Reckoning’ Breakout Portia Doubleday on Playing ‘White Girl Wasted’ Conspiracy Theorist: ‘I Knew People Who Were Radicalized’ By Daniel D'Addario Plus Icon Daniel D'Addario Chief Correspondent DPD_ Latest Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on ‘The Social Reckoning’: Getting Inside a Whistleblower’s Mind, Jeremy Strong’s ‘Antihero’ Zuckerberg and Why Trump is the Movie’s Voldemort 2 days ago ‘A Few Good Men’ on Broadway: Aaron Sorkin, Bradley Whitford and Team Behind Revival on Why It’s ’So Fucking Relevant’ in Trump Era 1 week ago ‘Adults’ Heartthrob Jack Innanen Reveals All: From Wildest Fan DMs to His Love for ‘Heated Rivalry’ to Whether He’d Shave His Iconic Mustache 1 week ago See All Leah Gallo SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “ The Social Reckoning ,” now playing in theaters. Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning” begins with a vignette about the impact of social media that’s as chilling as any statistic about the dangers of social media. And Portia Doubleday sits at its center, portraying the human toll of Facebook. In the first chapter of the new film, entitled “White Girl Wasted,” we see Doubleday’s character, Kaylee, standing by her stalled car on the side of the road. When two police officers (Sierra Capri and Michael Braugher) pull over and approach her, she tells them that AAA is on their way to assist her; she’s also visibly impaired, slurring her speech and combating them at every turn, even as her face is buried in her phone. Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Even as it seems the cops have nothing to go on — as she’s within her rights under California law to refuse to cooperate with their requests, they tell her they’re going to let her slide — Kaylee insists on intensifying the interaction, spewing racist and misogynistic invective at the cops and then capturing the consequences on video, declaring in a screeching monologue that she is “being treated like a fucking immigrant” and broadcasting it to subscribers of the “Voice of Reason” channel online. Popular on Variety This interaction, one that will feel unfortunately familiar to any viewer who’s spent time online this decade, sits at the heart of “The Social Reckoning.” Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” the 2010 film he wrote about the earliest days of Facebook, “Reckoning” confronts the world Mark Zuckerberg has brought into being. Kaylee is a person whose particular brand of rage could only exist in a post-social media world. After all, we learn she’s something of a changeling: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) knew Kaylee as a bleeding-heart leftist. By the film’s end, Frances has been so moved by Kaylee’s trajectory that she decides to spill the secrets of Facebook’s indifference to the harm it causes. Kaylee, meanwhile, joins the Jan. 6 insurrection. Doubleday may be best known for her work on USA’s Emmy-winning drama “Mr. Robot,” in which she played a conflicted employee at the series’ central villainous tech concern, E Corp. As she tells Variety , on the week of “The Social Reckoning’s” release, the way technology affects our cognition is a live concern for her, and has had direct consequences in her own life. When you first read the script, did you have a vision for Kaylee? Did she remind you of anyone or anything that you thought you might draw on? I live in Los Angeles, and I know what’s going on in the world. And I actually have known a couple of people who were radicalized, and they actually came to mind. During COVID, I was actually pre-med for like three seconds. Whoa! What? Yeah, there was nothing to do. But that’s a big thing to do. It was actually really difficult — cell bio is just excruciating. But I actually knew a couple people that were in the pre-med track and who were radicalized. And to know them so well and find that out was … I didn’t really understand. I think I still don’t quite understand how that happens. How can you understand the organelles of a human cell and understand what the scientific method is and how important facts are, and yet still believe that COVID can come from a 5G tower? I remember they were showing me these videos, and I couldn’t make sense of it. And so that’s kind of where I started with my own personal experience of what happens to a person. Repeated exposure can start to make extreme ideas feel normal. I kept thinking, “They’re in an echo chamber, and they’re seeing these really bizarre videos that look like they’re made in a basement, and they’re seeing them so often that I think they just have acclimated to the fact that there are these possibilities that they want to be in on.” They want to be cracking the conspiracy or these other truths that are not being examined. So I started there, and built from that place. I started to better understand how does a seemingly normal person turn out to be the one that you see in the beginning of the movie. What is that process like? That’s an interesting perspective, and one that I think is important in contemporary life and for this movie — that the radicalized are not some strange, naive other people, but people like you or I who fell prey to incredibly powerful technology. I think it’s the important perspective to have, because often I think that people see these videos and they think, “Oh, that’s a very faraway person. Something is wrong with them. They were raised and born that way.” That’s how I viewed it. You know, I viewed it as really away from me, and that’s not what happened. And so, having close relationships with people who were lovely and finding this out about believing in Pizzagate, I was really interested in the social science perspective of that. You know, what does gaslighting look like in human form? And I think that that’s also what [Kaylee] is in the movie, right? She’s the human component. What happens up close when one human is affected by this huge company’s massive influence? Or what can happen when you have that much power to influence the way that people think, especially when you’re giving them repeated exposure to certain ways of thinking? I interviewed Aaron Sorkin for a different story, and he mentioned that he’d had conversations with Frances Haugen, and that the character you play is drawn from a real story from Frances’ life. What were the conversations you had with him about Kaylee like? I think Aaron wanted it to be really grounded. That was really important, especially because — and we talked about this a lot — we didn’t want the moment to be about being under the influence, [as if] that is why this person is acting this way, but that this is actually how she feels. So we spent a lot of time grounding it and making sure that you saw what Frances saw with her friend, what we see online, and what my experience was with people that I’ve met that have just fallen into QAnon radicalization. It was really important that it felt real. A couple of things are happening that I think are easy to see: the entitlement and the victimization. Like she’s the victim in that moment; she feels perpetrated. And why is that? To dumb it down to “She’s a racist” would be reductive of what’s going on. That’s not really what that moment’s about. It’s: How do people, over time, change — especially with repeated exposure and influence? I remember watching these videos and thinking there’s something so emotional about it. It’s almost like an emotional addiction, and you become a part of a group, or you become a part of some way to vindicate yourself from your own pain or your own victimization by making somebody else the enemy to sort of justify the anger that you have within yourself. Those are the things that I brainstormed with him about because I was concerned [that it might] fall into this trap of “Oh, this drunk girl that’s just super erratic.” I want to talk about the nuts and bolts of acting the scene. Sorkin writes very rhythmic dialogue that is meant to be delivered note-perfect down to the comma. And, in the scene, you’re slurring your words. Did this present a special challenge? I was scared about that, actually. I remember Aaron sort of said this when we were rehearsing. He was like, “Just trust the words. They’ll save you.” Trust that you can land on them — and that is true. I don’t know how to explain it, but there is something unbelievably comforting, and I knew it when I read it, when I first got it … It infects your body, that rhythm. If you can get that rhythm in your body, it just feels like molasses. It just sort of runs together because he’s so brilliant. It affords the actor, actually, the ability to live within the constraints of words that you know are going to catch you. So instead of feeling like you might have to add or create a beat or figure out how to pull your truth out of a moment, he makes that process unbelievably effortless. We actually shot it in two days, which was lovely, because it was a pretty heavy scene, you know. How did you feel at the halfway mark, walking into night two? When the stakes feel this high when you’re working with someone, I just let myself feel. Because I trust him to know how to direct me, and he’s approachable and really funny and really warm, and what a joy to feel like “Hey, this lands.” I felt like I had the liberty to play a little bit. It was more about finding the level that he wanted. Where does that escalation begin, and why? Like, where is the moment where this person decides that they’re going to turn this night into what you saw? And I think that there is that moment where she’s sort of calculating; there’s like a moment where it turns, and I think he was really specific about that. I’m always nervous, but thankfully, he’s a great director, so that gave me the liberty to try different levels and see what worked and what didn’t. I’ve been comparing your work here to Rooney Mara’s at the start of “The Social Network”: It’s a one-scene performance, but it defines everything that follows, and we briefly glimpse each character again. In your case, you had to act as Kaylee storming the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. How did that feel to shoot? I remember Jan. 6 and how I felt that day, and … I never thought that I would be doing this. I never thought I would actually have to put myself in those shoes. And it made me really, really sad. I don’t want to get too emotional. It just made me really sad, because I had some space from it — especially given how loud things are, and there’s constant stuff going on every single day. But to actually be in that, there’s just something so tragic. That’s why I appreciated playing this character so much — because she’s a human consequence. She is the one who would be there. Behind amplifying extremism and misinformation and Facebook’s hand in this: What is this doing to one person that ends up being there? I was grateful to examine someone who has been part of what I’ve criticized — but it was really challenging. I had mixed feelings about it. Even that day, [Sorkin] kept saying, “Turn around and take in where you are, and [take in] that those people really believed it.” That’s what’s so gut-wrenching: [they’re] really believing that they’re doing the right thing. And that is what produces, for me, the anger and the rage and the sadness. That they feel how I feel when I’m standing up for something that I believe in. It’s the same. I first saw you on “Mr. Robot,” which was a show all about how the digital world is not separate from our real lives — it’s hopelessly intertwined with them, redefining reality. “The Social Reckoning” has similar concerns. Do you spend a lot of time thinking about these issues? Yeah, of course. I don’t really share too much online. I just talk to myself about how angry I am about things that are going on. And it’s interesting how people feel about AI, because watching this film, you see this person who may have had a good idea to connect people, and the consequences of it being this massive, and having this much influence and the ability to radicalize small groups of people who can actually cause a lot of harm. Where we’re at with AI, I feel like it’s really comparable. I don’t really think we fully understand the implications of what this is going to do to the world, and we’re sort of at the precipice. As a ’90s child, I’m just like, what is happening? The entire world is just going to massively change, and there’s going to be huge consequences to these changes. And who’s thinking about that? You know, like who’s ensuring that we’re actually going to be OK? That’s what I’ve been thinking about the most after “Robot.” I spend time concerned about it — I’m sure you do too. A lot of people do. Look what happened at Facebook. So what’s going to happen now with OpenAI? What is our future going to look like? We could discuss that for hours, and I think we’d emerge pretty dispirited. But I wanted to close the loop: What ended up happening with your pre-med studies? It was like the most incredible experience I’ve ever had. To be honest, taking the bio classes I took opened my brain to a whole different world. But I just was like, I still want to be an actress, and I don’t know if I can make a 20-year commitment . You know what I mean? I don’t know. Can I go 16 hours and just eat Top Ramen? I still think about it, though. It took me 20 years to finish my degree because my parents didn’t want me to become an actor. My dad was all about, you know, “If you’re stupid, you’re going to be evil, and you have to be smart.” And so it took me 20 years, but I got my B.A. — I took a little pre-med journey, and I finished! I’m not actually pre-med. But who knows what will happen? title: Kleber Mendonça Filho, Wagner Moura and More Brazilian Academy Members Release Open Letter Expressing ‘Concern’ Over Brazil’s Presidential Elections (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 7:25am PT Kleber Mendonça Filho, Wagner Moura and More Brazilian Academy Members Release Open Letter Expressing ‘Concern’ Over Brazil’s Presidential Elections (EXCLUSIVE) 'I'm Still Here' producer Rodrigo Teixeira, Alice Braga, Fernando Meirelles and Petra Costa are amongst signatories pleading for 'close international attention' to the upcoming second round in the polls between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Rodrigo Santoro and Camila Pitanga to Star in Marcelo Gomes’ ‘Garota da Urca’ From a Script by Luciana Paes and Leonardo Moreira (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Prime Video’s ‘Marília Mendonça – Sentimento Louco’ Offers Unparalleled Access to Brazil’s Most Popular Singer Five Years After Tragic Plane Crash 3 days ago Brazilian Cinema at Risk: A Report From Watching the Presidential Elections From the Rio Film Festival 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Cannes Film Festival Several Brazilian members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, including Oscar nominees Kleber Mendonça Filho , Wagner Moura , Emilie Lesclaux, Fernando Meirelles, Alê Abreu and Petra Costa, and Oscar-winning producer Rodrigo Teixeira (“I’m Still Here”), have released an open letter calling international attention to the upcoming second round of Brazil ‘s presidential elections. The polls will open Oct. 25 and see current president Luis Inácio Lula da Silva face far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year and three-month sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup d’état after losing the 2022 presidential election. Earlier this week, Variety published an in-depth report detailing how Jair Bolsonaro dismantled Brazil’s audiovisual sector, alerting to a similar future ahead if Flávio Bolsonaro wins the upcoming elections . Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Other high-profile signatories include Alice Braga (“City of God”), Karim Aïnouz (“The Invisible Life of Eurídice Gusmão”), Sônia Braga (“Aquarius”), Gabriel Mascaro (“The Blue Trail”), Carolina Markowicz (“Charcoal”), Anita Rocha da Silveira (“Medusa”), Anna Muylaert (“The Second Mother”), Laís Bodanzky (“Brainstorm”) and Rio Film Festival director Ilda Santiago. Popular on Variety The letter calls for “close international attention” to the elections, detailing how Flávio Bolsonaro has recently pledged “to rewrite Brazil’s 1988 Constitution” and noting an alleged U.S. intervention in the first round of the elections, reported by The Guardian in an investigation on how the “United States government allocated approximately US$1 million from a State Department human rights fund to a program called ‘Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.’” “We see the developments unfolding in Brazil as part of a broader pattern of alleged electoral interference across Latin America,” says the letter, which can be read in full below: An Open Letter from Brazilian Members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences to Our Colleagues in the Film Industry and the International Press We, Brazilian film professionals and members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in Hollywood, wish to express our concern over the current political climate in Brazil and call for close international attention to the second round of the presidential election on October 25. The margin between the two candidates in the first round was just 1.87 percentage points. Brazil is therefore a deeply divided country. We are nonetheless witnessing troubling signs of disregard for democratic norms, including allegations of possible foreign interference in Brazil that warrant transparent investigation and international scrutiny. The Guardian has reported that the United States government allocated approximately US$1 million from a State Department human rights fund to a program called “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.” At the same time, media observers have raised concerns about possible distortions in the reach of political content on Meta platforms and have called for an investigation. Among the cases cited are the Instagram accounts of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, which have reportedly experienced declines in reach, difficulties with access and visibility in search results, as well as an inability to promote posts through paid advertising. Another case involves a US-based website promoting the purchase of advertisements in support of candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in exchange for cryptocurrency tokens, under the promise of helping underprivileged children in Uganda. Brazil’s Federal Police are also investigating suspicions of cash payments to voters in rural areas. Several of Flávio Bolsonaro’s proposals also warrant close scrutiny, including his pledge to rewrite Brazil’s 1988 Constitution, which marked the end of military dictatorship and the restoration of democracy in the country. According to the candidate, a new constitution would be drafted by a Congress dominated by a far-right majority. This statement is particularly troubling in light of the attempted coup attributed to former president Jair Bolsonaro, the candidate’s father. The plot included plans to assassinate the current president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his vice president, Geraldo Alckmin. Jair Bolsonaro is imprisoned in connection with this case, while his son has pledged to grant him amnesty as his first act in office. Our concern is compounded by the way much of Brazil’s mainstream media has normalized these developments, failing to address with the seriousness they deserve the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro and the crimes attributed to his father. In addition to the attempted coup, Jair Bolsonaro was the subject of a complaint filed with the International Criminal Court in The Hague over the more than 600,000 COVID-19 deaths recorded in Brazil during the pandemic, amid actions and omissions by his administration. The complaint argues that more than half of those deaths could have been prevented. His administration was also associated with Brazil’s return to the United Nations’ Hunger Map. Now, his son is promising cuts to social security spending modeled on the austerity policies of Javier Milei’s government in Argentina. The omission or downplaying of these facts contributes to public misinformation and undermines the defense of democracy. As cultural professionals, we understand the cost these austerity policies can impose on our sector. Under the previous administration, Brazil’s audiovisual industry suffered from the closure of the Ministry of Culture, the suspension of the Audiovisual Sector Fund, the weakening of cultural institutions, and allegations of censorship. We fear a return to that scenario. Protecting freedom of expression and ensuring the long-term sustainability of Brazil’s audiovisual industry are inseparable from defending democracy. We see the developments unfolding in Brazil as part of a broader pattern of alleged electoral interference across Latin America. The defense of Brazilian democracy must therefore rest not only with the Brazilian people, through free, fair and transparent elections, but also with the vigilance and engagement of the international community. We call on the international press to cover this electoral process rigorously, on the international audiovisual community to amplify the debate, and on the relevant institutions to investigate these allegations independently. title: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Warns A.I. Models Are “Being Trained To Hijack Your Intimacy”
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Fashion Designer Bob Mackie Suffered Head Trauma In Fall Days Before Death – Report ‘Paranormal Activity’ To Haunt Broadway For Eight Additional Weeks Carla Gugino, Fred Hechinger, Tom Pecinka & Riley Prior Join Off Broadway’s ‘A View From The Bridge’ View All October 10, 2026 7:24am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Gordon Levitt at a press conference in the U.S. Capitol on February 4, 2026 Heather Diehl/Getty Images In a new video interview for The New York Times, actor Joseph Gordon-Levitt , serving as the United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance, has some concerning words about the impact of artificial intelligence. Things like the “decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy” and the hijacking “of your intimacy.” The video interview takes place as Gordon-Levitt is in en route to address world leaders and officials gathered at the U.N. on the impact of A.I. Watch the full video below. Related Stories Festivals ‘Artificial’ Review: Andrew Garfield Is Chilling As Sam Altman In Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI Origin Story That Should Make You Very Afraid – New York Film Festival News Aaron Sorkin Clarifies He “Was Never Asked” To Omit Trump From ‘The Social Reckoning’ But Film Is “Not A Red-Blue Thing” First question: Why should the public listen to an actor on A.I. safety? “Very fair question,” Gordon-Levitt responds. “Why listen to an actor? Don’t listen to an actor. You should read Human Compatible by Stuart Russell. Go look up Yoshua Bengio. Read posts by people who work in alignment and safety and policy. You don’t want to read all those things? Well, I did! So, you know, if you want to listen to me, that’s a shortcut.” Watch on Deadline Gordon-Levitt continues, “What we don’t want is a bunch of people confused or apathetic while these very fast-moving businesses design the future by themselves, just in the interests of their own profits. A lot of what needs to happen, I think, has to do with communication, which is ultimately kind of what acting or filmmaking is.” At one point in the direct-to-cell phone-camera interview, Gordon-Levitt is asked what he fears most about A.I. “At the risk of annoying The New York Times,” he responds, “I would object to that question just because reducing these concerns into one sound bite of fear — that’s one of the problems. To me, saying: Oh, I’m scared that A.I. could exterminate all of humanity — that doesn’t really get at the substance of the concern. There’s real validity to that concern. But that’s not the thing that really worries me. “The thing that worries me is a lot more complicated and a lot more boring to talk about, because it’s a lot more dense. The decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy. These companies are betting on the notion that they’re going to take over the entire economy. That would be totalitarianism, and that would be really bad.” He continues, “Simultaneously, these models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it. We shouldn’t be scared of an A.I. We should be concerned about the people building A.I.” When Gordon-Levitt, a co-founder of Creators Coalition on A.I. and recently named one of Time magazine’s 100 most influential “innovators, leaders, and thinkers” on the topic, is asked to explain the “human-centric digital governance” phrase in his U.N. title, the actor concedes “it’s sort of a mouthful.” “It just means that digital technology should be governed by people and for people,” he says. “’A.I.’ is nothing but algorithmically recombined, human-produced data. It’s humans. Calling it artificial intelligence sort of decenters humans. It offers this kind of magical fictitious character, this A.I. that we’ve seen in various sci-fi movies, but really — really all it is is us. It’s us.” On whether the “slow-moving” U.N. can force a “fast-moving” Silicon Valley to play by certain rules, Gordon-Levitt responds, “To be honest, this is one of the things that I have found sort of daunting or troubling. I don’t know the answer. I think if it does take, say, seven years for the U.N. to put together an internationally agreed upon regulatory framework for A.I., then seven years from now we’ll be glad that we started now.” ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie & Bacall ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $27.5M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted ‘Newlyweds’ Showrunner Gail Lerner Fired Ahead Of NBC Sitcom’s Premiere Read More About: Comments

title: Oscars: UK Selects ‘Rehearsals For A Revolution’ For Best International Feature Film
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi & Jimmy Chin Talk ‘Everest: The Other Side’: “This Is The Most Difficult Film We’ve Made” – Contenders London Symbioz Films Boards Cutthroat Istanbul Real Estate World-Set Drama ‘Sevda’ & Unveils Trailer View All October 10, 2026 7:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rehearsals for a Revolution Sony Pictures Classics The UK has selected Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals For A Revolution as its entry to the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards . The film explores Iranian filmmaker Ahangarani’s experience of exile as she rebuilds her life and creative practice in London, through five portraits of relatives and mentors, which are also expressions of resistance. The UK played an integral role in the film’s journey, serving as the base where it was written. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, Ahangaran retraces more than 40 years of Iran’s history. From the early days of 1979, until the war that began in 2026, she pieces together intimate and collective memories, forming the portrait of a country shaped by political repression and in constant hope for a revolution. Watch on Deadline The distributor said it will give the film qualifying runs in New York and L.A. in December. It will then open it exclusively at Landmark’s Nuart Theatre in L.A. and the Film Forum in New York on January 8, 2027, before rolling it out across the country over the following weeks. The deeply personal debut feature premiered as a Special Screening at the Cannes Film Festival where it won the L’Oeil d’Or (Golden Eye), and played last month at the Telluride Film Festival and Toronto International Film Festival. It was recently honored with an Albie Award from the Maysles Documentary Center, an award honoring those who inspire, not only through their work, but also through their roles as mentors, role models, and champions of social justice. “How extraordinary to see Pegah’s remarkable film recognized in this category. From winning the L’Oeil d’Or at Cannes to the standing ovations at TIFF and now this recognition, Rehearsals For A Revolution is building incredible momentum and marking a significant moment for a formidable female filmmaker creating in exile from her home country,” said SPC in a statement. “This selection in the Best International Feature category has the potential to be truly transformative for the film, opening doors to audiences around the world while shining a spotlight on Pegah’s extraordinary talent and her vital voice. title: Netflix’s ‘The Blue Road’ Director Han Jun-hee On Taking Risks With Stories & Shooting In Japan
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz AI Tools Bring Efficiencies But Have Limitations, Says Weta CTO Kimball Thurston: “Tech Companies Should Collaborate More With Creatives” ACFM Chief Ellen YD Kim Talks AI Development; Korean Recovery; Market Spotlights On Thailand & Japan Vietnam’s V Studios Seals Multiple Deals On ‘Red Woman’ Including Sales To North America & Japan View All October 10, 2026 7:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Blue Road Netflix Korean writer-director Han Jun-hee talked strategies for getting audiences to respond to risky or unfamiliar material in a masterclass at Netflix ’s Creative Asia day at Busan International Film Festival. “There has to be risk for something to be interesting. Only if you take risks can you tell an interesting story. Trying to play it safe all the time, especially in Korea, is a risk in itself,” said Han, who is involved in two series premiering in Busan’s On Screen section – The Blue Road , which he wrote and directed, and Dead-End Job , which he created. In a talk moderated by Netflix Korea content manager Kim Kijae, Han explained how he approached his breakout hit series D.P. (2021), about Korean military police on a mission to catch deserters, and Weak Hero Class (2022), about bullying and high school violence. Han wrote and directed D.P. while he served as creative director on Weak Hero Class . Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'La Bola Negra' Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: "Something Touched Deep Inside" - Contenders London Reviews 'Ray Gunn' Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird's Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup - London Film Festival “When it comes to army stories, some people think only guys can relate; but for female audience, they all have fathers or brothers who might have been in the army. If you think outside of the box, it could be an interesting story,” Han said. In the case of Weak Hero Class , which revolved around a group of male friends and features a lot of fighting, Han said: “In Korea, the perception is that this genre can only be made into a film with a small budget. And again, the story looks like it might only appeal to guys. But we all went through high school; met friends there, got jealous of someone, wanted to be someone; these are universal feelings. Then we also added action to the story.” Half joking, Han also said that casting a trio of hot, young actors – Park Ji-hoon, Choi Hyun-wook and Hong Kyung – was a conscious decision to draw in female audiences. But he also noted that all three have gone on to prove themselves as talented actors and big stars. Park starred in The King’s Warden , released earlier this year, which has become the highest-grossing Korean film of all time. Han also talked about the importance of working with new directors as he stepped back from the directing role for Weak Hero Clas s: “We have so many new talents emerging, so we can help them make something great, and by bringing in an emerging director, I knew Weak Hero Class would really shine.” Moving on to 2024 feature Pilot , Han described how he used genre, in this case comedy, to convey a message to the audience. Directed by Kim Han-gyul, the film is an adaptation of 2012 Swedish film Cockpit about a pilot who pretends to be his own younger sister after being fired from his job. “When we gave the script to the main actor [Jo Jung-suk], he responded in just three days. He said he wanted to try different things in comedy and felt this part could go deeper than being a superficial comedy role,” Han recalled. “With all the writers and directors I work with, if we take on something we’re not familiar with, we have to show that we understand it,” he added. “We can’t be prejudiced or biased. Whatever the story, I don’t think there’s a topic we can’t cover in a series or film. I don’t think you can say, ‘This isn’t commercial enough.’ If you have a message you want to convey to the audience, what is it you want to say? That is the most important part of filmmaking.” He took a similar approach when creating Dead-End Job , directed by Kim Da-min, which deals with a serious subject, the vagaries of the labor market, but also uses genre to convey a message: “When the scriptwriters first brought this to me, Netflix said it’s either going to be a short film or not work out at all. The story needed to be told in a familiar way to resonate with people, so that’s why we thought a fantasy element would be interesting.” Han also talked about The Blue Road , his return to directing, based on a manhwa about two detectives from Korea and Japan who form an alliance to track down a serial killer staging high-profile murders in both countries. While the two detectives have to navigate different working styles and jurisdictional hurdles, Han said the crews in the two countries also found they had to overcome cultural differences. “Korean crews are very fast and flexible, while Japanese teams are meticulous and prepare everything very carefully. Neither way is better or worse; just different,” Han said. “Japanese crew members all have unique roles to play and focus on getting everything perfect, while in Korean teams, we all help out on everything and do it quickly. If it doesn’t work out, we just try it again. At first, there were lots of misunderstandings, but we found we had a lot to learn from each other and eventually found a way to make it all work.” The Blue Road is streaming on Netflix from November 20, while Dead-End Job is scheduled for October 30. title: Brad Bird on Why He Took ‘Ray Gunn’ to Skydance Instead of Pixar: Making Animated Films for Teens and Adults ‘Shouldn’t Be a Controversial Decision’
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:55am PT Brad Bird on Why He Took ‘Ray Gunn’ to Skydance Instead of Pixar: Making Animated Films for Teens and Adults ‘Shouldn’t Be a Controversial Decision’ Skydance Animation's 'Ray Gunn,' directed by Brad Bird, will premiere on Netflix By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Brad Bird on Why He Took ‘Ray Gunn’ to Skydance Instead of Pixar: Making Animated Films for Teens and Adults ‘Shouldn’t Be a Controversial Decision’ 1 hour ago Shari Redstone-Backed Sipur Studios Opens London Office, Sets Out International Strategy Including Boarding Olivier Dahan’s ‘Nana’ (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Skydance-Owned Channel 5 Profits Dropped by $32 Million Last Year Due to Ad Market and Inward Streaming Investment 1 day ago See All Â©2026 Skydance Animation On a balmy April afternoon at Abbey Road Studios in London, a 74-piece orchestra comprised of violinists, cellists, flautists and even an organ-payer, is packed into Studio One. The iconic room, which has hosted musical legends from Edward Elgar to Harry Styles, is painted “Toy Story” blue, a fitting color given the reason everyone is here today is to record the score for “Ray Gunn,” a new feature animation from Pixar legend Brad Bird , the brains behind “Ratatouille” and “The Incredibles.” Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year The film, which has been gestating inside Bird’s mind for three decades, is not a Pixar or Disney project, however (more on which later), but a Skydance Animation production which will hit Netflix on Dec. 18 (it premieres at the BFI London Film Festival on Oct. 10). Popular on Variety Directing the orchestra at Abbey Road is Bird’s longtime collaborator, composer Michael Giacchino . “ Ray Gunn ” is the duo’s sixth project together since first teaming up for “The Incredibles” in 2004 and it’s one Giacchino (who won an Oscar for Pixar’s “Up” in 2010) has had more than two decades to prepare for. “We talked about this movie during ‘The Incredibles,’” the composer reveals, when we speak a few months later. “I’ve known about this for a very long time.” Fittingly, given the key role of music in the film , Bird first conceived the idea for “Ray Gunn” – a noir detective caper set in a “Jetsons”-style retro future – after hearing The B-52s’ song “Planet Claire.” To Bird, the tune sounded like a mash-up between the theme song to 1960s detective series “Peter Gunn” and “a ’50s monster sci-fi movie,” Bird says in an interview a day before the film’s premiere. “I went, ‘This is not “Peter Gunn.” What is this?’ And then I went, ‘It’s Ray-Gun.’ And then I went, ‘ Ray Gunn : It’s a guy’s name. He’s a detective, but it’s in the future.’” Michael Giacchino and Brad Bird (courtesy of Netflix) Courtesy of Netflix But the idea got shelved as other projects got in the way: there was his sophomore Pixar project “Ratatouille” followed by “The Incredibles 2” and, in between, live action fare “Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol” and “Tomorrowland” as well as an abandoned attempt to adapt Will Eisner’s comic “The Spirit.” Bird, who describes his mind as a “big shop floor,” would come back and “tinker” with “Ray Gunn” every now and again, biding his time until he could bring it to life (the film fell through at other studios including Warner Bros.) It was “Mission: Impossible” that finally paved the way for what had effectively become Bird’s real-life mission: impossible. “It was [Skydance’s] second film and everybody was happy with how it turned out,” Bird says of his turn at the helm of the Tom Cruise franchise. So when the opportunity arose to pitch the studio on another idea, “Ray Gunn” was the obvious choice. (The move also reunited Bird with Pixar co-founder John Lasseter, now the head of Skydance Animation .) “I never pitched it at Pixar because I felt like it wasn’t in Pixar’s wheelhouse exactly,” Bird explains, referring to the studio’s reputation for catering to younger audiences than the one he’s aiming at with “Ray Gunn.” “If you put a Pixar label on it people would go, ‘Oh well, it’s meant for the same audience that these other films were meant for,’ and inevitably some of them would go, ‘Well, my little Jimmy would be unhappy at this.’” Bird expands on the theme, pointing out there are “10 billion animated films” for children and far fewer for teenagers and adults, despite them comprising the majority of the movie-going audience. Making animated films for them “shouldn’t be a controversial decision,” Bird says, “and yet it was always treated that way by the ministers of resource allocation [at Pixar].” (He is returning to Pixar for his next project, a third “Incredibles” movie.) Skydance had a different take. “My thought when [they] got involved was that that they’ll go with me on this slightly different audience tangent,” Bird says. “And here it is.” Skydance CEO David Ellison is a producer on “Ray Gunn”: was that in name only or was he fairly hands-on? “Well, he was more involved in the earlier days,” Bird says. “But he got — you know, his plate became very full.” The director is obliquely referring to Ellison’s recent battle to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery . Bird won’t be drawn on whether he thinks Ellison will stick to his promise, made as part of his bid, that Skydance will produce at least 30 theatrical films a year . “All that stuff is beyond my pay grade,” he says, sidestepping the question. While Skydance may have become the latest lightning rod in an increasingly polarised and under pressure Hollywood, Bird is a pragmatist. Later in our conversation, he notes that after making “The Iron Giant” he took his nascent idea for “The Incredibles” to Pixar. “The crew from ‘Iron Giant,’ a lot of them were mad at me initially because they felt like I was leaving hand-drawn [animation] and going to the sexy new CG,” Bird recalls. “And I said I don’t really care about the technology part. I’m going up to Pixar because they protect storytelling.” “Ray Gunn” Netflix As it happens, protecting — versus exploiting — art is one of the themes of “Ray Gunn,” which follows the eponymous private detective (voiced by Sam Rockwell) as he uncovers a dastardly plot involving Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), a superstar singer with a huge secret. For Giacchino, the trick to scoring a film filled with so much intrigue is keeping the viewer guessing. “Probably the second toughest thing was just making sure everything was always in alignment thematically, so that I didn’t give the audience something that they shouldn’t be thinking about,” he notes. (The actual toughest, he says, was an intimate scene between Gunn and Nova when they’re first opening up to each other. “It needed to really hit every single emotional beat in this perfect way,” he explains.) Bird may have written “Ray Gunn” almost three decades ago but it’s themes of art, technology and corporate greed resonate now as much as they did in the late 1990s. He says the screenplay changed “less than you’d think” between that first draft and the finished movie. “A lot of the things that people are saying that [the film] is dealing with that are contemporary right now in the headlines were in there 30 years ago,” Bird notes. “People are people and greed is greed and the flaws of people make good subject material for films. If that’s what’s driving the story, then the story’s not going to age because it’s about eternal things rather than things that were in the news last week.” New York Comic Con Unveils 2026 Professional Schedule Lineup, Including ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ Author-NBCUniversal TV Panel (EXCLUSIVE) Amazon Viking Drama ‘Bloodaxe’ Sets Release Date, Debuts Fierce New Trailer at New York Comic Con Chase Infiniti to Star in Dylan Clark’s ‘Portrait of God’ at Lionsgate With Sam Raimi and Jordan Peele Producing Blumhouse Atomic Monster Inks Short Film Development Deal with Horror Creator Heidi Wong ‘Helluva Boss’ Actor Lashes Out at NYCC Heckler: ‘I’m Going to Jump Over This Fence and End You’ As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Loading comments...

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi & Jimmy Chin Talk ‘Everest: The Other Side’: “This Is The Most Difficult Film We’ve Made” – Contenders London Symbioz Films Boards Cutthroat Istanbul Real Estate World-Set Drama ‘Sevda’ & Unveils Trailer View All October 10, 2026 6:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Antonia Blyth, Javier Calvó, Javier Ambrossi, Penélope Cruz, Guitarraicadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau and Carlos Gonzalez on the panel for "La Bolsa Negra" at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Vianney Le Caer, Deadline Spanish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi delved into the generational trauma behind award-winning film La Bola Negra at Deadline’s Contenders London . The feature – revolving around the interconnected stories of three gay men in 1932, 1937 and 2017 – took its cue from Alberto Conejero’s 2013 play La piedra oscura , which in turn was inspired by García Lorca’s unfinished play La Bola Negra . At the heart of the La piedra oscura is the love story between real-life football player Rafael Rodríguez Rapún and Lorca during the Spanish Civil War. The work is spun into another story in the film about a young trumpeter called Sebastián, played by singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente. Related Stories Reviews 'Ray Gunn' Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird's Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup - London Film Festival News 'Project Hail Mary' DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The "Most Complicated" He's Ever Shot -- Contenders London “When I read in the plane the first monologue, I started to cry… something touched deep inside, like a wound I didn’t know I had about like my country and what happened like 90 years ago,” he said. Watch on Deadline He and Javier Ambrossi then investigated Lorca’s play and discovered it was unfinished. “We realized it was the first play he was going to portray a gay character, so it was going to be revolutionary. But he was murdered. He couldn’t do it, and we were like, ‘What a loss!’” The directorial duo went to Granada to consult the screenplay which is preserved at the Centro Federico Garcia Lorca. “We got to see the four pages and there was like a power in those pages, like art as a physical thing, because the niece of Lorca said that fascism wanted to destroy all the manuscripts when the war started, but everyone hid it. So, it felt like a weapon that fascism wanted to destroy. We start from there, imagining what ‘La Bola Nera’ could have been, mixing it with ‘La pieda scura’, and then we had our present timeline.” Ambrossi said the four pages had acted as a character blueprint for their film. “The beautiful thing about the four pages that exist of the unfinished work by Federico Garcia Lorca is that the first page is a list of characters he was going use,” he said. “It was like a challenge, you know. I was like, oh my god, if we reimagine this world, it could be something very beautiful.” Penélope Cruz , who has a small role as Nené Romero, a Cuplé singer entertaining soldiers during the Spanish Civil War, also joined the conversation. Cruz said she was a big fan of the directors’ work – which includes The Messiah and Veneno – and instructed her to set up a lunch. “Like after 10 minutes we were friends and then they told me they were writing this movie, and there was a character that they thought about sending, but they thought it was too short. And I told them never worry about that with me. Like I don’t choose the material based on how many minutes the character is on screen,” she recounted. “A few days later they sent it, and I completely fell in love with the Nené, and I was blown away by this script. title: Six-Armed, Two-Legged Spider Princess Tale ‘Migali’ Unpacked by Its Director Ahead of MipJunior World Premiere
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:45am PT Six-Armed, Two-Legged Spider Princess Tale ‘Migali’ Unpacked by Its Director Ahead of MipJunior World Premiere Ahead of the premiere, Director Cédric Frémeaux shared his memories of the journey that has been bringing this loveable character from page to screen in an ambitious 52x11-minute series, premiering this fall on TF1, RTBF, Ketnet and RTS. By Kevin Giraud Plus Icon Kevin Giraud Latest ‘The Smurfs’ Season 4 Gets First Look as Peyo Productions Reunites With Nickelodeon, RTBF, Ketnet, KiKA and TF1 (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago In a Groundbreaking Premium Drama, ‘R91’ Brings a Murder Mystery Aboard Flagship French Aircraft Carrier 3 days ago BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe’s Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum 3 weeks ago See All 'Migali,' a spider princess with heart. Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS At MIPJunior , it’s not often that a little creeper gets put out on center-stage. But on Oct. 10, as “ Migali ” makes its world premiere in front of buyers from all across the globe, a tiny spider princess seems to be set on weaving webs of laughter and fun at the unmissable Cannes children’s TV market. Produced by Adelaïde Terme ( Easy Peasy Entertainment , the production/licensing arm of French Auzou Publishing Group) along with Bardaf! Productions in co-production with RTBF , Ketnet , RTS and TF1 , “Migali” is a 52x11minute series centered on six-year-old Migali, a spider princess determined to become queen. Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS As she heads to the Royal Academy, where princes and princesses of all kingdoms learn to control their abilities, Migali brings her boundless energy and extraodinary web-weaving skills to the school, meeting a gallery of other quirky characters from all size and shapes. Facing (and, more often than not, provoking) chaos in her daily life, Migali stays happy, merry and positive, meeting each challenge as a new, fun adventure. Popular on Variety An adaptation of the eponymous comic book series by Alexandre Arlène and Fabien Ockö Lambert, “Migali” is directed by Cédric Frémeaux (“50/50 Heroes”). Ahead of the premiere, Frémeaux spoke with Variety about the smooth journey that has been bringing this loveable, quirky spider princess from page to screen. “I’ve always loved animated series,” recalls the storyboard artist-turned director. “As a kid, I woke every morning eager to discover ‘Dexter’s Laboratory,’ ‘Dragonball,’ and many others. I was captivated by these worlds. Growing up, it quickly became clear to me that I wanted to work in that industry someday.” During high school, Frémeaux found his way as an intern at Ankama, the French multimedia giant behind videogame hit “Dofus,” subsequent animated series “Wakfu” and manga hit “Radiant.” After studying animation at LISAA in Paris, he started his career as a storyboard artist, dabbling with editing and directing on trailers and teasers. “Migali” is his second series, a match made possible by Terme, who reached out to Frémeaux for this adaptation. “She presented me Auzou’s line-up, and I immediately connected with ‘Migali,’ which turned out to be her own pick for our collaboration. What struck me with this character is how radiant and fun she was, as a heroin. With our target audience [kids 5-8], it’s very important to connect with a protagonist. And with Migali, they definitely can as she faces the sames challenges that they do.” Migali, who Frémeaux frames as “Spiderman’s young cousin living in a world of unicorns, dragons and potions,” was brought to screen in close connection with the author duo and Terme, who saw the potential for an animated series even before the first comic was published. Since then, Migali’s books have sold more than 150,000 copies in France, and boasts nine volumes already. This success fueled Frémeaux’s enthusiasm even more, as he prepared himself for the challenge of bringing this character to the screen. “What I also love about ‘Migali’ is its humor, which doesn’t shy away from deeper topics that really connect with kids. Children from this age are much smart than we think, and if you’re lazy in your writing, they will see it instantly. Today, they have access to so much content. They know these narratives, and they know how it works. Instead of fighting for their attention span with fast-paced, frantic content, we chose to craft something that both takes them seriously and makes them laugh. And I think that’s key to succeeding in retaining kids’ attention today.” Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS Yet, as Frémeaux continued, the challenge of producing 52 episodes of 11 minutes (or as he put it, a nine-hour movie) was a huge undertaking. “Once storyboard was locked, we had to deliver a full episode’s animatic every week. And to do that, there’s only way I know: surrounding yourself with talented people who understand the project.” Frémeaux goes even further: “My role as a director is to find people who are better than me at they own field of expertise. Once I managed to achieve that, every piece fell right into place, and the production was very smooth.” A production that was split between Caribara studios in Annecy, Paris, and Caribara Belgian subsidiary Waoooh. “The key is these large European co-productions is to communicate constantly, and maintain overall cohesiveness throughout the whole pipeline. Animation is, at its heart, a collaborative art, and I strongly believe ‘Migali’ benefits from this collective effort. It would be a far less interesting product if I had created it alone with AI tools.” “Migali” is AI-free, as the teams received strict instructions during this creative process. While aknowledging its uses, Frémeaux views AI technology as a tool that can’t be part of creating something. “Technology has always been part of the animation industry, which faced similar issues with the introduction of 3D, and other tools that revolutionized the medium over and over. But creativity has to remain at the center of this process, and tools can’t replace artists. Our show is made by people who asked themselves a lot of questions, who made choices in framing, staging, and poured their craft and soul in this series. And that is something that AI can’t do.” Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS As “Migali” premieres this afternoon, Frémeaux is eager to present this colorful, quirky character to the world. “Much like in our show, Migali is about to discover a whole new world, and I can’t wait to introduce her to global audiences. The series has a lot of potential, and we’ve only scratched the surface of Migali’s universe. There are many more paths and characters we can explore, to build beyond the Royal Academy and introduce children to this loveable IP.” “Migali” premieres today at MipJunior, subsequently airing on TF1 and other partner broadcasters in the following months. The series is distributed internationally by Moon-Keys International Content. title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell and Scarlett Johansson in Brad Bird’s Forgettable Netflix Animated Neo-Noir
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All October 10, 2026 6:45am 'Ray Gunn' Courtesy of Netflix Ray Gunn ( Sam Rockwell ), private eye, is special. He’s “the only honest player in a crooked game,” the only dick who prioritizes things like truth and justice over cold hard cash. In a retrofuturistic society where aliens are disdained as second-class citizens, he’s the rare human who stands up for extraterrestrials. Some scorn him for his heroism; others admire him for it; all agree he’s something of an oddity. Ray Gunn , Netflix’s new Skydance Animation feature from Pixar alum Brad Bird , is not special. It’s a blandly palatable jumble of sci-fi and neo-noir clichés, not so much awful as underwhelming. Lacking in both visual pop and emotional specificity, it’s a forgettable entry in an otherwise rich career that’s run the gamut from Ratatouille to The Incredibles to Mission: Impossible — Ghost Protocol . Related Stories Movies John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell Buddy Up for London Film Festival Premiere of 'Wild Horse Nine' Movies Brad Bird on Finally Making 'Ray Gunn,' His Live-Action Run and When Things Turned Political at Disney Ray Gunn The Bottom Line A bland pastiche. Release date: Friday, Dec. 18 (Netflix) Cast: Sam Rockwell, Scarlett Johansson, Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, Kether Donohue, Michelle Rodriguez Director: Brad Bird Screenwriters: Brad Bird, Matthew Robbins Rated PG, 1 hour 59 minutes The screenplay, by Bird and Matthew Robbins, assembles paper-thin characters in service of a PG storyline that’s simultaneously too simplistic for adults and too serious-minded for kids. In the bustling city of Metropia — think 1940s Manhattan but with hovercars and jetpacks — Ray is a detective so hard up for cash that his office gets a little emptier every time he returns to it, his coat rack and his couch and then his desk getting repo’d one by one. Ray’s problem is not a dearth of skill, but an overabundance of conscience. He’s such a mensch that even as he’s fleeing from a dangerously botched job, he can’t help but stop to rescue the gangster who’d just been trying to murder him. “These things, why do you do them?” groans his partner, a spindly one-eyed being named Eye-Ra ( Tom Waits ). But Ray’s fortunes seem set to change once he’s hired by MegaMax studio head Vogel (Alan Tudyk) to wrangle Venus Nova ( Scarlett Johansson ), the studio’s biggest musician. All Ray has to do, to the tune of three times his normal rate, is keep the famously volatile artist out of trouble. The best way Ray can think of to do so is to tail her shady husband, Dom (Bobby Cannavale) — all the way into a sordid (but still vaguely family-friendly) web of deceit, murder, blackmail and gangland drama. The first thing you notice about Ray Gunn , basically as soon as that Netflix rainbow disappears in the opening seconds, is that it looks … fine. Metropia, with its bright gleaming surfaces, evokes a Disneyland-ified version of the cities in The Fifth Element or Blade Runner . Ray and Venus are pretty, but in an unremarkable way you wouldn’t be able to pick out of a lineup. The rare memorable details — like the glazed-porcelain skin on an alien mob boss (Matt Berry’s Slugsy), so vivid it looks almost tactile — only serve to highlight how textureless and weightless and frankly cheap the rest of the film looks. The action is zippy, as anything involving bodies falling hundreds of feet or hovercars crashing through glass office buildings is bound to be, but for the most part not especially inventive. The exception is a shootout that flirts with body horror thanks to a malfunctioning blaster; it’s a surprising burst of creativity that will leave you wondering where that energy was the rest of the time. The indistinctiveness of the visuals is matched by the broadness of the characters and story. Ray, despite being the protagonist, has no personality beyond “good,” and only the vaguest suggestion of a backstory. (One of the few details we learn is that he’s a disgraced cop … but only because he’s such a good guy that he was made to take the fall for an actually corrupt cop.) Venus is not much more than your standard-issue troubled starlet — screaming at her husband in public, fighting with the paps — until suddenly she develops a whole other personality out of nowhere that feels completely disconnected from the first. At least her original music is passable, even if the narrative context surrounding it can’t help but evoke Netflix’s much more successful KPop Demon Hunters . (Kimbra wrote and produced her songs; the score is by Michael Giacchino.) The lone standout in the ensemble is Eye-Ra, voiced by Waits with a weariness that adds some sorely needed wit and weight to this too-slick world. He’s decent enough to admire Ray’s moral compass but pragmatic enough to suggest bending it a bit from time to time, and consistently funny enough to make this conundrum amusing. “We are months away from being able to afford ethics,” he complains after Ray turns down yet another shady payday. While the plot gestures at potentially rich themes like xenophobia, corporate corruption, the perils of celebrity and even the looming threat of artificial intelligence, Ray Gunn has not much to say about any of them beyond that they’re bad. One would imagine a scene like one in which Ray is forced to take a grievously injured Eye-Ra to an alien-only hospital after the human-only one refuses him service would take a beat to reflect on the cruelty of Metropia’s segregationist policies. Instead, the film rushes past it so quickly it’s all but forgotten just minutes later. In at least one instance, all of Ray Gunn ‘s biggest shortcomings converge in the most leadenly predictable of ways. A character’s complete and utter blandness becomes a major plot twist, which might scan as clever if not for the fact that it’s signaled so blatantly, anyone half-paying attention will surely have guessed the big reveal roughly 60 minutes before it’s confirmed. Bird has said he’s been trying to make this project happen since before The Iron Giant , which I suppose makes this a professional triumph for him if not a creative one. But I can’t decide if that explains its mediocrity — this feels very much like a first draft of a project — or makes it all the more baffling that with decades to mull it over, he hasn’t managed to make it more interesting. title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:45am PT ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm Freely borrowing from past films including ‘Who Framed Roger Rabbit?,’ ‘Blade Runner’ and ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ this Netflix outing impresses technically, but it’s short on laughs and heart. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm 1 hour ago ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck Returns to the Director’s Chair for a Nasty, Compulsive Kidnapping Thriller 2 days ago ‘Krux’ Review: A Potently Bleak Portrait of German Village Life at the Bitter End of WWII 3 days ago See All Skydance Animation/Netflix “Welcome to the future,” we hear several times in “ Ray Gunn ” — not that the brave new world it presents is all that welcoming. Or, for that matter, particularly brave or new. The good news is we finally have flying cars and superpowered jetpacks; in other respects, though, we haven’t come a long way at all. Co-existence with extraterrestrials has seen humans revert to old habits of prejudice and apartheid; crime and corruption are rampant as ever; pop-up ads now irksomely manifest as holograms in your personal space. Still, at least the future looks good. The fifth animated feature from Brad Bird is a handsome return to the retro-futurism he previously practiced in “The Incredibles” and his live-action oddity “Tomorrowland”: in this case, a vision of an impossible 21st-century metropolis as might have been dreamed in 1939. Related Stories How to Stream the 2026 MTV VMAs Live Online Taylor Swift to Be Honored at 2026 MTV VMAs With Inaugural Artist-Director Award The world-building — indeed, even just the building-building — is the principal ongoing thrill of “Ray Gun,” as it zips restlessly between gorgeous Art Deco skyscrapers, smokily lit Old Hollywood nightclubs and vividly kitsch rent-a-rooms, all rendered in chic, clashing scarlets and lilacs and burgundies, in vehicles that may be futuristically engineered, but have the luxurious, elongated curves of pre-WWII automobiles. Like “Blade Runner,” Bird’s film sits in the genre-melding realm of sci-fi noir; unlike “Blade Runner,” with its seamy, rain-sodden transformation of Los Angeles, this lighter, brighter detective story is not willing to sacrifice much gleam. Popular on Variety And fair enough: “Ray Gunn” is a caper first and foremost, with all its gumshoe antics safely in the PG-rated zone, though one suspects many of today’s kids may be entirely bewildered by it. (After all, Robert Zemeckis’ peerless “Who Framed Roger Rabbit?” — the original and best repurposing of noir tropes for family entertainment, and a clear creative touchstone here — is now very nearly as old as the 1940s classics it was spoofing.) Bird’s mystery zigs and zags breathlessly as it probes multiple murders connected to a femme fatale -styled starlet in the imaginary city of Metropia; it’s consistently nifty, even when it feels less than original. But it it’s never quite as funny as it should be, while its characters — in particular the eponymous hero, a smooth-talking P.I. voiced by Sam Rockwell — want for texture and soul. Audiences should happily speed along with them on their adventures, but after a fairly long two hours in their company, we don’t feel terribly attached to them. These aren’t fatal shortfalls: There are more than enough visual and sonic delights here to compensate. But they are surprising ones from Bird, whose animated work has been marked by zingy, non-snarky but adult-favoring wit and carefully seeded personal stakes. In “Ray Gunn,” the titular pun — the protagonist’s name, but also his preferred weapon — is typical of the script’s quippery, getting more nods and smiles than outright giggles. The only character dynamic worth a damn, meanwhile, is that between Ray and his weary partner Eye-Ra (Tom Waits, the film’s most inspired casting coup, yielding its most affecting voice performance), who run a down-at-heel “discreet investigations” business from a creaky office being gradually stripped bare by repo men. Business is bad for Ray, in part because Eye-Ra is an alien cyclops, and human-alien collaboration is frowned upon in this world. (We never learn how the two species came to occupy the same planet, but the law regarding their separation is entrenched: Eye-Ra is barred from human hospitals, while aliens can only enter certain clubs as serving staff.) It’s a heavy racial allegory to throw into an otherwise breezy enterprise, and the tone hiccups here and there as a result. With more than a nod to the identity politics that underpinned last year’s “KPop Demon Hunters,” however, it does eventually figure into the principal storyline — which, after a couple too many introductory false starts, kicks off when Ray is hired by Arnold (Bobby Cannavale), the lunkhead fourth husband of tempestuous pop megastar Venus Nova ( Scarlett Johansson ) — to spy on her, though his motivations, of course, aren’t entirely what they seem. When people start showing up inconveniently dead and she’s thrust into scandal on the eve of her new album launch, Ray finds himself effectively babysitting her whilst carrying out his own snooping. But she’s a hard woman to pin down, in multiple senses; the more he knows about her, the less he knows about her, and naturally something sparks between them. It’s an odd, perhaps youth-pandering detail that Venus, with her wasp-waisted silhouette and Veronica Lake hairdo, isn’t a Hollywood siren but a Dua Lipa-style electropop artist. (Her original songs are in fact written by Grammy winner Kimbra, of “Somebody That I Used to Know” fame, and they aren’t much in dialogue with Michael Giacchino’s wonderfully busy, brassy score, which makes no secret of its preferred era.) Nova’s particular brand of celebrity doesn’t really fit the film’s 2039-by-way-of-1939 mission statement, though it does allow Johansson a standout torch number in a more anti-period-appropriate vein — when Venus shows her true colors. Turns out she, like Bird, wants everything old to be new again, or everything new to be old again, or whatever the case may be. She has a suitable partner on that front in the analog-inclined, trenchcoat-sporting Ray, but his image, too, doesn’t entirely add up: Rockwell voices him with jaded slyness, but he has the unlined face and swooshy hair of a Disney prince, rather than any stubbly Bogart gruffness. It’s just one reason why we can’t altogether warm to him — and why he doesn’t light up the center of Bird’s beautifully rendered dark-pastel dystopia. Rather like the man himself, “Ray Gunn” has slick, boundless energy and resourcefulness to spare, but that doesn’t quite amount to charm. ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, Oct. 8, 2026. title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird’s Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup – London Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck And Kerry Washington Fight A Lot In Netflix Kidnap Thriller That Is Stretched Too Thin ‘The Social Reckoning’ Review: Jeremy Allen White And Mikey Madison Expose Facebook In Aaron Sorkin’s Stirring Journalistic Thriller Sequel ‘Artificial’ Review: Andrew Garfield Is Chilling As Sam Altman In Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI Origin Story That Should Make You Very Afraid – New York Film Festival View All October 10, 2026 6:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Ray Gunn' Skydance Animation If David Ellison wants a ticket to the Oscars this year it most likely won’t be with anything from Paramount or even (so far) from Warner Bros, but if you said Netflix you might be on the right track. Ray Gunn , from Oscar-winning filmmaker Brad Bird ( Ratatouille, The Incredibles ) , comes out of Skydance Animation ‘s original deal with the streamer, counts Ellison among its producers, and is the kind of smart, visually sumptuous and clever ‘toon that is ripe for the Best Animated Feature category. Having its world premiere Saturday at the London Film Festival, Ray Gunn is a throwback to Bogart-style film noir detective classics like The Maltese Falcon, The Big Sleep and other ’40s gems of the Dashiell Hammett, Raymond Chandler and Sam Spade mode. Throw in a little Chinatown via Jack Nicholson or Altman’s The Long Goodbye, or Robert Mitchum in Farewell My Lovely, and you get the idea, and then think elements of The Jetsons or Who Framed Roger Rabbit animated hits, marry them with Blade Runner, and then toss in a bit of Madonna in Dick Tracy, take a visit to the Star Wars bar, stir them all together and you have something approximating the world Bird has cooked up here. In other words it is a love letter to the movies past and futuristic. They call its main setting, Metropia, an “alternate future” channeling 1939, and that seems about right. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Brad Bird On The 30-Year Journey To Bring ‘Ray Gunn’ To The Big Screen — London Film Festival Culture The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office No matter what the inspirations, and there were clearly many, they all come from cinema and that’s a delicious thing here. Bird, who also wrote the nifty script with Matthew Robbins, has been blessed to collect a sensational voice cast to match an intriguing bunch of characters who make up this mashup. Chief among them is Sam Rockwell ‘s Ray Gunn, an analog private dick in a digital planet. The methods he uses are mainly all AI’ed in this futureworld, but he operates like its San Francisco circa 1941, handling cases with his partner in grime Eye Ra Kadock (a wonderful Tom Waits ), a cyclopian alien at the ready for any assignment that comes their way. And boy do they get a doozy when sultry Venus Nova ( Scarlett Johansson ), a troubled pop superstar, walks in the door. Of course its all about a murder she is accused of, one of her ex-husbands, and the timing couldn’t be worse for her beleaguered record company Megamax, now run by her first hubby and manager Barry Vogel (Alan Tudyk). Gunn is hired to keep her out of trouble, something she constantly finds herself in. Could there also be an instant attraction here? They don’t need the scandal or the nagging competition from Slugsy (Matt Berry), an alien mob boss who would like to bring Venus back under his purview. There are all sorts of sides to Venus, a lot of shady characters complicating things, and in pure Bogie-Bacall fashion Ray gets to sort them all out while dealing with this colorful group. Using vibarant CGI techniques to bring this world to life, Bird and his talented artisans manage to successfully merge two very different worlds, centuries apart in a cohesive and viable original universe that somehow seems right. You don’t have to be a fan of noir and Dark City detective yarns to appreciate the story, and it doesn’t matter if you aren’t a sci-fi aficionado either. The human/alien blend blends and helps to make this Skydance Animation production an entertaining proposition for adults and even their kids who get dragged to see it, rather than the usual other way around for ‘toons.

full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:25am PT Prime Video Takes Global on Turkish AI-Generated Movie ‘Çukur:Vartolu,’ a Spin-Off From the Hit Series Known Internationally as ‘The Pit’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Prime Video Takes Global on Turkish AI-Generated Movie ‘Çukur:Vartolu,’ a Spin-Off From the Hit Series Known Internationally as ‘The Pit’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Margherita Ferrari on Working With Paolo Sorrentino on Directorial Debut ‘Föa — Once Upon a Future’: ‘He Helped Me Pursue and Protect My Vision’ 1 day ago ‘Elsinore’ Producer Andrea Occhipinti on Bringing Ian Charleson’s Story to the Screen and His Personal Connection to the AIDS Crisis: ‘I Lost a Lot of Friends’ 2 days ago See All Çukur:Vartolu Courtesy AI Yapim Prime Video has taken global rights to Turkish TV powerhouse Ay Yapim’s AI movie “Çukur: Vartolu,” a spin-off from its hit series “Çukur,” known internationally as “The Pit.” “Çukur: Vartolu” is produced by Ay Yapim under its Singapore-based artificial intelligence studio AI Yapim that in August launched the AI-generated historical drama “Castle Walls” also on Prime Video, in what was touted as the first show made end-to-end with AI to bow on a major global streamer. While the original “Çukur” follows the Koçovalı family and the Istanbul neighborhood under its control, where family loyalty intersects with the criminal world, the spin-off turns to the childhood and choices that shaped Vartolu Sadettin, who is the Koçovalı family’s illegitimate son. “After losing his mother and grandfather, a boy grows up on the streets, waiting for his father to find him,” says the film’s synopsis. “When that hope gives way to revenge, Salih becomes Vartolu. Yet his desire to settle the past shapes decisions whose consequences reach beyond him.
