title: Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo On Directing Rwanda’s Oscar Submission ‘Ben’Imana’: “We Need To Understand What Happened” – Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Wildwood Director’ Travis Knight On LAIKA’s Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic: “It Took Us 16 Years To Make This Movie” – Contenders London Deadline’s Contenders Film: London Kicks Off With A Dozen Buzzy Awards-Season Movies John Leguizamo Boards Colombian Cycling Documentary ‘Cyclovia’ As EP View All October 10, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo on a panel for 'Ben'Imana’ Deadline It’s been a good year for Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo; after directing the first Rwandan feature to be accepted into the official selection by the Cannes film festival, where she was awarded the Camera d’Or, her film Ben’Imana was recently nominated as the country’s first ever Oscar submission. Set in 2012, 18 years after the genocide against the Tutsi, the film unfolds in a Rwandan village where survivors and perpetrators are grappling with the process of reconciliation. Speaking at Deadline’s Contenders London event, Dusabejambo, who was seven at the time of the genocide, revealed that she had turned to cinema after studying mathematics and physics. Several short films ensued, but the idea for Ben’Imana came after the second, in 2013. “I think it was my destiny, but it was a film that was still trying to find expression in me. I needed time to understand, to feel, to read, to hear… There’s a point in time where in every generation needs to understand what happened, where we came from, what happened, and what people decided to do in their time within their own means to be able to continue.” Related Stories News Oscars: Rwanda Makes History As 'Ben'Imana' Becomes First Official Entry; Alexander Set U.S. & UK Release News Indie Media Outfit Alexander Opens Film Arm With Kevin Chan, Hamish Moseley On Board And 'Ben'imana' Set As First Release It was important, she said, to break through the myths and preconceptions that have sprung up around the genocide. “I wanted to be more authentic to the history,” she said, “and I also wanted to not judge the people, the generation, that came before us, and what they did. I didn’t really want to fall into the stereotype of the victim and the perpetrator. All of this was about turning our lives around, making peace, being able to create a future and put a mirror to my community.” Watch on Deadline In wrapping up, Dusabejambo praised her crew and mostly non-professional cast for bringing her story so vividly to life. “I love that the film looks like a million dollars,” she said, “but [it didn’t cost] a million dollars. The million dollars comes from the love and the art and the will of the people who worked with me to tell the story… There were many times when the fictional elements of the story were meeting the reality, because it’s 100% made by Rwandans. All of us, we are connected to this story.” Check back Monday for the panel video. title: ‘Project Hail Mary’ DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The “Most Complicated” He’s Ever Shot — Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Léa Seydoux & Marie Kreutzer On The “Earthquake” At The Heart Of ‘Gentle Monster’ — Contenders London Danny Boyle On The Challenges Of Rupert Murdoch & ‘The Sun’ Film ‘Ink’: “We Had A Siege Mentality While Making It” — Contenders London Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Starring In Addiction Dramedy Series ‘Quitters’ For Angel View All October 10, 2026 5:51am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Greig Fraser and Charles Wood at Contenders London Deadline Oscar-winning DoP Greig Fraser knows a thing or two about working on challenging movies, from Dune to The Batman , Rogue One to Zero Dark Thirty . At Deadline’s Contenders London event today, the in-demand cinematographer revealed that none were as challenging as Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s space hit Project Hail Mary : “This was the most complicated film I’ve shot,” the Australian native disclosed. “Every day was the most complicated day,” he explained. “How do you capture a puppet without a face in a rolling circle with no gravity. Then there are stairs and steps to factor in. Everything was a challenge, but an awesome challenge.” Related Stories News Penélope Cruz On Working With Javier Bardem In Florian Zeller's "Bunker": "We Knew Florian Was Never Going To Manipulate Anything From Our Real Relationship" -- Contenders London News Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In 'The Liberation': "Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?" -- Contenders London In the film, Ryan Gosling plays science teacher Ryland Grace “who wakes up on a spaceship light years from home with no recollection of who he is or how he got there. As his memory returns, he begins to uncover his mission: solve the riddle of the mysterious substance causing the sun to die out. He must call on his scientific knowledge and unorthodox ideas to save everything on Earth from extinction…on the journey, an unexpected friendship means he may not have to do it alone.” Watch on Deadline Sandra Hüller, Lionel Boyce, Ken Leung, Milana Vayntrub co-star in the Amazon MGM crowd-pleaser, which took $684.5M at the global box office. Fraser and the film’s production designer Charles Wood, also known for his work on blockbusters including Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Avengers and Guardians Of The Galaxy franchise, talked about how the film was grounded in authenticity and not overly saturated in VFX. Wood explained: “A lot of the sets were eight to 10 foot in diameter. So the camera was on everything. Greg’s camera was on everything. I needed to make sure that whatever was in front of the camera really gave the audience a feeling that you were really in this ship with this man going to eternity.” Fraser added: “There was an authenticity to the rationale of how things operated. There wasn’t anything created for the sake of visual pleasure. It started in a place of honesty from a science perspective, which is how the book’s written.” That desire for authenticity included the puppetry work behind the film’s memorable alien character Rocky. Wood commented: “I didn’t realize coming onto the film that this would all be essentially live action. Working with a team of puppeteers on a set of a certain diameter was a real challenge. I wasn’t even sure how it was all going to play out, but it’s extraordinary how the puppet team did their work. It shines through in the film. You feel this creature really did exist.” Fraser said he recognized the film’s comparison with E.T. , another film celebrated for for relying on practical effects and animatronics rather than computer-generated imagery (CGI). “The times there are VFX, they’re stunningly, authentically appropriate for that particular part of the film. I think that the the directors have found that same through-line with this film. They’re used for an absolutely good reason.” As part of their research Wood described how the team met NASA astronauts and heard about their experiences, including how one was so overwhelmed by seeing the earth from space that he would cry but his tears wouldn’t fall due to gravity, meaning he often had a blurred vision of the planet from his ship. Fraser and Wood were both asked about the potential for a sequel or follow-on movie given that the book’s writer Andy Weir has spoken about writing another novel connected to the story. “That’s the first I’m hearing about it”, Fraser said. The movie is produced by Amy Pascal, Gosling, Lord, Miller, Weir, Aditya Sood and Rachel O’Connor. Max Morales / Netflix ©2026 “ Under Siege ” (“Palacio”) the fictional series inspired by the storming of Colombia’s Palace of Justice by an M-19 guerrilla commando and its subsequent retaking by the Colombian army, bows Nov. 6 on Netflix . The events, which unfolded in the capital of Bogotá on Nov. 6 and 7, 1985, is recounted in the eight-part series directed by a troika of directors comprising Edgar Nito (“The Gasoline Thieves”), Samir Oliveros (“Bad Lucky Goat”) and Guatemala’s Jayro Bustamante (“La Llorona”), whose latest feature, “Mountains of Fire” (“Cordillera de Fuego”) represents Guatemala at the Oscars , his fourth bid at the golden statuette. Popular on Variety The next day, the Colombian Army stormed the Palace and retook it, resulting in the deaths and disappearances of at least 94 people, including justices, guerrilla members, civilians and military personnel. It also follows the victims’ families in their pursuit of justice for more than two decades. Produced by veteran Colombian producer Dynamo (“Narcos”), which celebrates its 20 th anniversary this year, and backed by more than seven years of exhaustive research based on archives, testimonies and interviews, the series follows multiple angles and related events to build a rousing narrative experience. Written by showrunner Natalia Santa (“ One Hundred Years of Solitude ”) along with Enrique Videla (Lucia Puenzo’s “La Jauría”), Enrique Lozano (“Virus Tropical”), Jenny Ceballos (“Wild District”) and Estefanía Piñeres (“Ruido”), “Under Siege” was mostly filmed in Bogotá on a set spanning more than 4,000 square meters (43,000 sq. ft) that took more than three months to build. Production also included a 30-meter structure recreating the original façade of the Palace of Justice, according to Netflix. In an earlier interview, Netflix’s VP of Latin American Content Francisco Ramos described it as “a huge undertaking, even by our own standards…and we’re of course, going to take it through what happened through the coup attempt,” stressing that authenticity is key at Netflix. This is likely Netflix’s second most ambitious project in Colombia after its adaptation of Nobel Laureate Gabriel García Márquez’s “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” which wrapped its second and final season on Aug. 26, and involved the building of an entire backlot to represent the legendary town of Macondo. I t is among a slew of projects that Netflix has been producing in Colombia , buoyed by the incentives and burgeoning talent pool of the country. The “Under Siege” cast includes Natalia Reyes (“Terminator: Dark Fate”), Carlos Manuel Vesga, Robinson Díaz, Luna Baxter, Mariana Gómez, Santiago Alarcón, Nicole Santamaría, Andrés Castañeda and Camilo Amores, among others. title: Penélope Cruz On Working With Javier Bardem In Florian Zeller’s “Bunker”: “We Knew Florian Was Never Going To Manipulate Anything From Our Real Relationship” — Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In ‘The Liberation’: “Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?” — Contenders London Brad Bird Talks Long-Gestating Passion Project ‘Ray Gunn’ & Portraying “Characters Who Are Desperate” In Utopia — Contenders London Oscars: Democratic Republic Of Congo Selects ‘Rumba Royale’ For Best International Feature Film Race; The Fally Ipupa Starrer Is Country’s Second Ever Submission View All October 10, 2026 5:36am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Florian Zeller and Penélope Cruz on the panel for "Bunker" at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Vianney Le Caer Florian Zeller and Penélope Cruz stepped into Deadline’s Contenders event in London where the duo discussed their upcoming psychological thriller, Bunker . The film, which Zeller wrote, produced and directed, sees Cruz star as the wife of her real-life husband Javier Bardem as their characters face emotional and moral challenges in an increasingly uncertain world. Bardem plays Miguel, a successful London architect, who considers a prestigious offer to build a survivalist bunker for a tech billionaire. The project causes his wife Sofia (Cruz) to question their relationship of 17 years as they are drawn deeper into a life of extreme wealth, paranoia and fear. The intrusion of an unsettling neighbor becomes another source of anxiety. Related Stories News Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In 'The Liberation': "Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?" -- Contenders London News Siân Heder & The 'Being Heumann' Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment -- Contenders London Zeller says that it was “a dream” of his to work with Bardem and Cruz. “I was interested in working with them together because I thought it would be an opportunity to explore something unique as a couple in life and also, to question what it is to be together and to explore love, to explore forgiveness in a long-term relationship through these extraordinary talents.” Watch on Deadline Cruz admitted that making the step to play a fictional couple in a feature film was a big one for her and Bardem, as the pair had made the decision “not to work together very often.” “We thought about it a little bit because, of course, the temptation was huge because we both love Florian,” said Cruz. “We love his work so much, but we always said we were not going to work together very often because it is a way to protect the relationship. I think it would be too risky to work together to often. But when we read it, and when we spoke to him, we looked at each other and really didn’t see any reason to say no. We both wanted to do it, and we knew that Florian was never going to manipulate anything or try to force anything from our real relationship into the movie.” Cruz added that a week before their “big fight” scene in the film, which was shot across three days, “things started to happen and I started to feel weird.” “Of course, it was because that scene was coming,” she said. “But I always said to myself, ‘that’s not possible, it cannot be because that scene is coming.’ We are old enough to not let that affect us, but it did affect us.” Cruz added: “But it’s just a natural process to find some truth.” Zeller noted that the fight scene, which is an almost 11-minute scene, is somewhat “the core of the film.” “It encapsulates thematically and emotionally everything the film is about. For a long period of time during the film, Penelope’s character is going through a crisis, but you don’t really know exactly what it is. Something is missing but she cannot exactly know what it is until that moment comes when she starts to become very vocal about it. So that’s a moment that is very key emotionally in the film.” Additional cast in Bunker include Stephen Graham, Paul Dano and Patrick Schwarzenegger. The French-Spanish co-production is produced by Federica Sainte-Rose and Zeller for Blue Morning Pictures, Fernando Bovaria and Simon de Santiago of MOD Producciones and Alice Dawson. Pathé’s Ardavan Safaee and Mediawan’s Pierre-Antoine Capton serve as co-producers. Check back on Monday for the panel video. title: Naomi Ackie Discusses “Hollywood Machine,” Her ‘Star Wars’ Experience and Buying a Crank Radio
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 10, 2026 5:14am Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Naomi Ackie in ‘I Love Boosters’ Courtesy of Neon Naomi Ackie ( I Wanna Dance With Somebody , Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker , Small Axe , Mickey 17 , The Thursday Murder Club ) stars in Boots Riley’s anti-capitalist satire I Love Boosters , part of the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF), which runs through Oct. 18. But on Saturday, she discussed not only her new film, which features her opposite the likes of Keke Palmer, Demi Moore, Don Cheadle and Taylour Paige, but also her broader career experiences and insights into the acting profession during an LFF Screen Talk. During the session, moderated by Grace Barber-Plentie, BFI London Film Festival programmer, the star repeatedly drew applause and laughter from an adoring crowd that left the room buzzing about Ackie’s passion and natural charisma. Related Stories Movies 'Bedford Park' Star Moon Choi Charts Her Own Path Between Korea and Hollywood Music Lisa and Director Sue Kim on Documenting the Star's Break From the K-pop System in 'Always Lalisa' One recurring theme was the actress’ seamless move between smaller U.K. productions and Hollywood movies, as well as between film and series. Ackie shared that she enjoys this variety of opportunities but also acknowledged that she feels most at home in the U.K. capital’s industry circles. “The London film scene feels like home,” and running into old friends and acquaintances feels “so comfortable,” she told the audience. “I feel, controversially maybe, [that] in America, it feels like Hollywood, and Hollywood is not a thing that I’m particularly stimulated by. It’s a machine, and I respect it, but it’s not necessarily the thing that makes me feel the most comfortable.” She also offered that when it comes to awards season, the big U.S. and U.K. awards are also different. For Oscars, actors are often making a lot of appearances, making the process similar to a presidential campaign and more predictable, while BAFTA nominations seem more surprising to her, Ackie said. Barber-Plentie pointed out in the context of the star’s thoughts on the Hollywood machine that many of the U.S. directors that Ackie has worked with started with smaller independent films. The star shared that this may also explain one of her recent favorites. “I’m obsessed with Obsession ,” she told the London audience. “You look at that director [Curry Barker] – he’s been doing YouTube shorts for the longest time!” Speaking of horror movies, Ackie mentioned that she was off to L.A. later in the day to start promoting Clayface . “Has anyone seen It Follows ,” she also asked, drawing many shouts of “yes” from the crowd. “The sequel [ They Follow ], I just finished this summer.” Her approach to genre films: “I just love doing horror because it’s actually the funniest job,” she told the LFF Screen Talk. “I said to my team: ‘Guys, maybe I should ease up on the horror.’ Horror is popping right now. It’s the best genre right now.” Ackie also offered her take on what has been driving the popularity of horror films, namely war and other horrors in the news. “I think it’s because, as a global community, we are extremely anxious. Did you see that tornado in Sydney?” she said before sharing her own worries. “Also, everyone, get your tins! Please, get your tins of food and your water. I’m not even joking. I bought a crank radio. … And the candles. I’ve got matches, magic straws just in case the water gets dirty.” The actress emphasized, though: “I’m afraid, but I don’t want to put that on you.” Ackie didn’t only discuss horror, but also comedy during her appearance, including I Love Boosters . “I love a female friendship,” she offered in expressing the joy she felt on the set. “Representing female friendship is a special thing.” A special experience of a very different sort was, of course, her work on Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker . She recalled how she felt she wouldn’t get the role, as she has done after various other auditions, only to get a surprise call back. But the actress highlighted that even Star Wars and other big roles didn’t change certain things for her. “It didn’t change me from the inside,” she explained. “I still live exactly the same, and that was eye-opening.” Ackie also shared on Saturday that the, or one of the, hardest roles she has ever taken on was playing Whitney Houston in I Wanna Dance With Somebody . “I’m a perfectionist, and this shit sent me crazy because you can never know a person,” she recalled. “It was something about the pressure of people knowing Whitney, people loving Whitney, me playing her. Am I good enough? This is a mountain. I remember saying to my sister: ‘I feel like I’m a baby looking at the top of a mountain, and somehow I need to crawl up to the top.'” Concluded Ackie: “It was probably the most difficult part, but I look back at the film now, and I’m like: ‘Good for you!’ That’s probably one of the favorite things I’ve ever done. The reviews weren’t the most incredible; the box office didn’t do great, but for me personally, it changed my approach to my craft. Because once you do something like that, I was like: ‘Give me anything!’ … Because I know I’ve probably done one of the hardest things I can in my life.” At 35, Ackie has done so many different things, but there are some roles that she would like to take on in the future. Recalling how she grew up loving West Side Story and Grease , the actress said: “I really would love to be in a musical. I just love it. It offers so much joy to me.” She also recalled how her character in Lady Macbeth , opposite Florence Pugh and Cosmo Jarvis, becomes mute halfway through the movie. “It taught me that we communicate a lot with our bodies and not with the words we say, and I still use that to this day,” Ackie said. “I was chatting to Lashana [Lynch] the other day, and I was like: ‘My dream is to do a film where I don’t say anything.’ And she said: ‘Me too.’ I feel like a lot of actors might feel that way.” THR

title: Léa Seydoux & Marie Kreutzer On The “Earthquake” At The Heart Of ‘Gentle Monster’ — Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Léa Seydoux & Marie Kreutzer On The “Earthquake” At The Heart Of ‘Gentle Monster’ — Contenders London Danny Boyle On The Challenges Of Rupert Murdoch & ‘The Sun’ Film ‘Ink’: “We Had A Siege Mentality While Making It” — Contenders London Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Starring In Addiction Dramedy Series ‘Quitters’ For Angel View All October 10, 2026 4:57am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Léa Seydoux and Marie Kreutzer at Deadline's Contenders London Deadline/Scott Garfitt Gentle Monster writer-director Marie Kreutzer and star Léa Seydoux took to the stage at Deadline’s Contenders London event to discuss the journey behind their Cannes drama. Seydoux plays Lucy, an experimental pianist who moves with her beloved but panic attack-liable husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) and young son to a rural farmhouse in Bavaria. Life seems swell until a special unit of big-city police led by Detective Kühn (Jella Haase) swoop in and seize one of Philip’s devices. As expected, they find and seize thousands of images of child pornography — and his double life is exposed. Catherine Deneuve plays Lucy’s mother in the feature. Related Stories News 'Project Hail Mary' DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The "Most Complicated" He's Ever Shot -- Contenders London News Penélope Cruz On Working With Javier Bardem In Florian Zeller's "Bunker": "We Knew Florian Was Never Going To Manipulate Anything From Our Real Relationship" -- Contenders London The project has a striking resonance for Kreutzer. In 2022, the Austrian director released Corsage , starring Vicky Krieps and Florian Teichtmeister. The following year, Teichtmeister was arrested and pleaded guilty to possession of child pornography: 76,000 files spread over 22 devices. He received a suspended sentence, which outraged many Austrians horrified by the crime committed by a prominent cultural figure. Inevitably, Kreutzer’s film was tarnished by association and even withdrawn from some cinemas. Watch on Deadline How did that experience shape Gentle Monster ? Kreutzer explained today that she “started working on Gentle Monster in 2020, after reading an article in a German newspaper about a ring of criminals being uncovered in Germany. So when all that happened with the actor, I knew so much about the issue, and it was a very disturbing coincidence. I thought, ‘I can’t make the film anymore’, because it will always be connected to an actor, but sometime later, I realized it’s maybe more of a reason to make the film and to confront it and not run away from it.” Seydoux described why she was drawn to the film: “I loved the script. I thought it was well written and and very subtle, because the subject is obviously a tough subject, and it’s not that easy to make a film about a subject like this one. I love the fact that it was told through the woman’s perspective, and that it’s through her eyes that the the story formed. It’s not through the victim’s perspective or through the perpetrator’s perspective. I thought that was extremely interesting because I was able to to express very contradictory feelings and a large range of different emotions.” She described the revelation at the heart of the movie as “a horrible thing” that creates “an earthquake inside” her character. The actress said that among the most challenging practical aspects of the film were speaking German and the concert scenes where she has to play the piano. Kreutzer agreed that the concert scene was among the most difficult to capture: “The big concert scene was a really hard thing for for both Lea and me because she’s a very intuitive actress, which I love, and I’m a very intuitive director, and less technical. I know what I need to know, but I don’t want any marks for the actors, I want them to move freely, so don’t plan shots in millimeters. That’s not how I do it. And so when you’re shooting a scene like that, you have to do that. It was a day where I felt like it was out of my hands and I can’t really do anything and everyone’s really stressed.” Kreutzer also described a “wild day” when Seydoux, who doesn’t drive, had to drive a car in reverse with a child in the back seat. Netflix acquired the film as Cannes was wrapping up in May and opens it October 30 in limited release before it starts streaming on November 18. title: Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In ‘The Liberation’: “Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?” — Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In ‘The Liberation’: “Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?” — Contenders London Brad Bird Talks Long-Gestating Passion Project ‘Ray Gunn’ & Portraying “Characters Who Are Desperate” In Utopia — Contenders London Oscars: Democratic Republic Of Congo Selects ‘Rumba Royale’ For Best International Feature Film Race; The Fally Ipupa Starrer Is Country’s Second Ever Submission View All October 10, 2026 4:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Guy Nattiv and Carrie Coon on the panel for "The Liberation" at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Vianney Le Caer Writer-director Guy Nattiv and actress Carrie Coon joined Deadline’s Contenders London event today where the pair discussed making The Liberation , a very personal story inspired by real events from Nattiv’s own grandmother. The film, which Bleecker Street is releasing in in the U.S. in January, is set in the early 1980s where Rita, a depressed New Jersey bank worker and Holocaust survivor (Coon), is lured into an all-female woodland commune by a charismatic leader (Lily James), while her daughters attempt a rescue. “I was only eight when my family took me to seminars to see my grandmother and participate with her in those meetings,” said Nattiv. “I didn’t know what it meant. It was like dancing with people in the dark. I heard horrific stories from people, and my grandmother crying, it was so weird to me. But no one told me what it was exactly, and I didn’t know until I became a teenager when my family had basically broken in front of my eyes, and my grandmother left my grandfather, left our family, and just joined this. Now, we know it was a cult but at the time we didn’t know what it was.” Related Stories News Siân Heder & The 'Being Heumann' Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment -- Contenders London News 'Wildwood Director' Travis Knight On LAIKA's Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic: "It Took Us 16 Years To Make This Movie" - Contenders London Nattiv said that when he was older and was processing these events as a film student, he started asking a lot of questions but didn’t get a lot of answers. It was a decade ago that he decided to take his camera and visit the cult after his grandmother had passed away. “I asked questions and I got answers…ish.” Watch on Deadline He entered the process with “a lot of empathy” and found that the cult “tried to free her” from her trauma of being a Holocaust survivor. “She had the courage to do something very uncommon: To leave your family, say goodbye to your daughters and your husband and go into the unknown and try to save yourself.” Coon admitted she was “absolutely fascinated by the story” and said she watched “hours and hours” of footage from Yad Vashem and from Shoah Foundation testimonies, “particularly women from Poland,” to help her research for the role of Rita. “There’s something very specific about the way the recounting of those unspeakable things is held in the body,” said Coon. “And also, the stories themselves, the myriad forms of trauma that were inflicted upon people. But then also that they were resilient enough to survive was also very fascinating and people had a find a way to survive and Rita had a very particular idea about what that looked like for herself…who are we to say what is required for someone to move on?” Coon continued that it was helpful for her to view the story as “a love story.” “What I became very fascinated by with reading is the idea that these social rules we are living by are tacit agreements,” she said. “There’s nothing written down. We wake up in the morning and we’re a wife and a mother and we follow all of these rules. But it’s all made up. We could essentially walk away from our lives at any time, but we don’t do it. And we did [in this film]. I just find that brave and shocking.” Check back on Monday for the panel video. ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $27.5M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted ‘Newlyweds’ Showrunner Gail Lerner Fired Ahead Of NBC Sitcom’s Premiere Read More About: Comments

title: Netflix Romance ‘Love Untangled’ Director Namkoong Sun on Netflix Freedom and the Funding and Distribution Gap in Korean Indie Film
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 4:36am PT Netflix Romance ‘Love Untangled’ Director Namkoong Sun on Netflix Freedom and the Funding and Distribution Gap in Korean Indie Film By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Netflix Romance ‘Love Untangled’ Director Namkoong Sun on Netflix Freedom and the Funding and Distribution Gap in Korean Indie Film 3 hours ago AI Can Cut Film Budgets by Up to 40%, Says ‘The Outlaws’ Director Kang Yoon-sung, as Netflix Reveals Use on 300 Titles: ‘A Human Touch Is Absolutely Essential’ 5 hours ago Busan Market Chief Ellen Y.D. Kim Plots Year-Round ACFM 365 Platform, Warns Public Funding Has Stalled 5 hours ago See All Naman Ramachandran Namkoong Sun , director of Netflix ’s Korean romance “ Love Untangled ,” said her first commercial feature felt little different from her independent films once cameras rolled, apart from the scale. The freedom, she added, came with weight. Namkoong was speaking at “New Voices in Film,” an industry panel staged by the Busan International Film Festival and Netflix as part of Creative Asia, alongside Ryu Eun-jung and Song Kwang-min, the married co-directors of the short “My Aunt.” Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Namkoong’s first two features, “Ten Months” and “Time to Be Strong,” were independent titles released in theaters. She joined “Love Untangled” when the project and screenplay were already in place, coming on at the adaptation stage, and said the offer landed just as she wanted to find joy again after two films about thorny social problems. A little over a year passed between opening the production office and release. Popular on Variety “Once we went into production, it was a system where we could focus only on the film,” Namkoong said. “There may be upsides and downsides to that. I didn’t want to imagine what would happen if I failed to take responsibility within that freedom. But because that freedom was there, there were definitely things I was able to bring to it.” Netflix staff sat in on meetings and worked inside the team throughout, she said, and the changes to the script were her own, made in service of what she saw as the film’s theme of happiness. The story is set in 1990s Busan, and with a modest budget for a period piece, the production recreated the Gwangan Bridge under construction to give the film a sense of place. Her message to younger directors was that a director always carries responsibility for the story, “but within a space where creative freedom is guaranteed, I think you have to take that responsibility really seriously.” Namkoong said she missed crying and laughing with audiences and cast in theaters, a ritual a streaming release doesn’t allow. “Once it was out on Netflix, people all over the world were watching it at the same time. On Twitter, Instagram, all kinds of social media, everyone flocked in and enjoyed it together, me included,” she said. “Small, sweet romance films don’t make up a big share of the Korean audience. But I was getting messages from people in Brazil and friends in Poland and Colombia saying the film was popular there.” The film reached No. 1 in many countries and stayed in the global top 10 for more than six weeks, she said, even though it was made in Korean and is “really just a Busan story, a very local story.” Her earlier releases had harder luck with timing. “Ten Months” premiered in the first year of the pandemic, with festivals shut and cinemas at half capacity. The press screening for “Time to Be Strong” took place on the day martial law was declared in Korea. “We did all the press, went home excited, and then that happened that night, so our news disappeared,” Namkoong said. “My Aunt” is a 24-minute short. It follows a dog groomer looking after an abandoned dog over the course of one day, when the niece she raised 10 years earlier turns up at her door. It won three prizes at this year’s Mise-en-scène Short Film Festival, where Namkoong served on the jury. It is streaming on Netflix in Korea until December as part of the platform’s showcase of the festival’s prizewinners. Ryu, who also plays the lead, drew on her own childhood, when she was raised by her fifth aunt, who later took in an abandoned dog. She had no plans to act in it but, having worked as an actor before, took the role herself and asked Song, her husband, to co-direct. Song handled directing on set, the pair shared storyboarding in pre-production, and Ryu led post-production. A previous collaboration had involved shouting matches over the phone, both recalled. This time, both said, speaking to each other without a filter built trust. Song said he had first felt torn about a Netflix release, given what cinemas offer in image texture and sound, but came to see it as a stroke of luck. On a film-rating app, his previous film drew responses from about 15 people. “My Aunt” has been logged by 7,000 to 8,000 viewers, with more than 1,000 comments. Namkoong, who was once a Mise-en-scène breakout herself, described the festival as a launchpad for the next generation of Korean directors. “These days, unlike in the past, anyone can upload their film to YouTube. You can screen it anywhere, really,” she said. “But what we do is pick out films and say, these are films that are more like real cinema, these are the films we’d like people to see, and put them on a list somewhere. When that came together with Netflix, the impact became huge.” Asked by an audience member to name the single biggest challenge facing Korean independent filmmakers, the three directors answered in turn. “The difficulty in the independent film world, then and now, is raising the budget. But more than that, the biggest challenge is not knowing in advance where a film will go after it’s made,” Namkoong said. “Even when a film is shown at a festival, you can’t tell whether it will get a release, because of what a release costs and various other things. We manage somehow to get it made, but there isn’t the infrastructure, like theatrical infrastructure, to show it.” Ryu said cost was her main worry with “My Aunt” too. “Independent film is film made independently of capital, so it has to be made with the individual creator’s own money,” she said, noting that platforms for indie film, and interest in it, remain limited. Song, who has always paid for his films himself, named capital as the biggest hurdle but said he had no other complaints. “Shooting films is so much fun. I loved it.” All three are now writing screenplays for their next projects. title: Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment — Contenders London
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment — Contenders London Mike Leigh, Marion Bailey & Kate O’Flynn On The Close Collaboration Behind ‘Tender Loving Care’ — Contenders London Society of Composers & Lyricists Opens First International Chapter In London View All October 10, 2026 4:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin J. Walsh, Sian Heder, Ruth Madeley, Adam Caldwell and Bernard Telsey at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Scott Garfitt/Deadline “I think we created history,” Being Heumann producer Kevin Walsh concluded this morning during a Q&A session at Deadline’s Contenders London . The veteran producer wasn’t speaking specifically about the feature film, but the accessible environment he and director Siân Heder created on the film’s set. “We are as proud of that as we are of the movie,” Walsh continued. The Apple Original Films title tells the true story of disability-rights advocate Judy Heumann, played by Doctor Who alum Ruth Madeley . Based on Heumann’s memoir, it centers on the year 1977, when Heumann led more than 100 disabled people to take over the San Francisco Federal Building, kicking off a 28-day sit-in — the longest occupation of a federal building in U.S. history. Related Stories News Mike Leigh, Marion Bailey & Kate O'Flynn On The Close Collaboration Behind 'Tender Loving Care' -- Contenders London News Brad Bird Talks Long-Gestating Passion Project 'Ray Gunn' & Portraying "Characters Who Are Desperate" In Utopia -- Contenders London The protesters form a tightly bound community, refusing to leave until the government enforces Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which required all federal spaces to become accessible. Watch on Deadline “We really approached this film with the same kind of relentlessness that Judy approached her life,” Walsh said. “We had 10 disabled leads. It took a lot of detail to make it accessible. Making ramps that were accessible with trailers, retrofitting hair and makeup trailers for disabled actors to be able to use. It took a company like Apple to really support us.” Discussing the origins of the project, Heder said a friend who worked on the Sundance documentary Crip Camp , which starred the late Judy Heumann, tipped her off about Heumann’s life story. “A friend of mine was the accessibility coordinator for Crip Camp at Sundance, and she sent me a text message and said, I’m hanging out with this woman, Judy Heumann. She’s the coolest woman on the planet, and someone should make a movie about her,” Heder explained. “I’d had a very profound experience on Coda , entering the deaf community and really understanding how many of these stories aren’t told. There are so many of these incredible stories within the disability community, and they are just never represented.” Heder said she later saw Crip Camp and read Heumann’s memoir, which introduced her to the story of the 504 protests. “I was just really intrigued by Judy because she’s so funny. She was this little woman with this Brooklyn accent. She was so self-possessed and so hilariously in command of everybody,” Heder said. Being Heumann debuted last month at TIFF and screens this week in London as one of the London Film Festival headline galas. title: ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’
full_text: Oct 10, 2026 4:16am PT ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ By Ophélie Surcouf Plus Icon Ophélie Surcouf Latest Netflix’s ‘The Blue Road’ Director Han Jun-hee on Why Playing It Safe Is the Real Risk 4 hours ago Vietnamese Horror ‘Arithmadtic’ Leads Bee Entertainment’s Busan Market Slate, With New Film From ‘The Corpse’ Director 11 hours ago Yoon Dan-bi’s Toronto and San Sebastian Film ‘The World Before’ Gives Its Camera a Soul and Its Island a Voice 4 weeks ago See All Netflix When Kim Ji-yong read the script for “ Possible Love ,” its emotional climax, set in a still forest by the beach, had no wind in it. Korean summer storms on location changed that. The cinematographer behind “Decision to Leave” and “Squid Game” Season 2 asked director Lee Chang-dong to change the scene’s setup, a choice that ended with crew members shaking the trees with ropes. Related Stories Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Taylor Swift Still Has Unfinished Business With Her Exes — Thank God! — While Also Mooning Over Her Groom in 'The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore': New Tracks Review Delivering a masterclass titled “Cinematography of Possible Love: Quiet, Yet Deeper” at Netflix ’s Creative Asia program during the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), Kim detailed how he and Lee built the film’s look around natural light, and how much preparation that choice required. “Possible Love,” Lee’s first film in eight years, won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize at Venice last month and is South Korea’s submission for the international feature Oscar. It screens in BIFF’s Icons section ahead of its Netflix launch on Nov. 6. The drama follows two married couples from opposite ends of the economic ladder: Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) and her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), and documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). Popular on Variety For all the film’s naturalism, almost nothing in it was left to chance, not even the weather on the day of the climax. The team prepared for every windy day announced by Lee’s favorite weather YouTube channel. “And every time, the director would say, ‘There is such a thing as a film ghost,’” Kim told the audience. “But that ghost only appears and helps once we have prepared thoroughly past 100% and put in all our effort.” The ghost never showed up. Instead, everyone on set except the five or six crew members needed to shoot went into the woods, tied ropes, hung onto them and shook the trees. “The film ghost did not appear. But our staff ghosts on set created this,” Kim said, calling it one of the most memorable moments of his more than 20 years in film. That tension between the natural and the constructed ran through the lighting too. “Ultimately, the balance was centered on supporting natural light, using film fixtures only to assist,” Kim said. In day scenes, film lights were only used where natural light fell short; at night, the team relied as much as possible on existing streetlights and lamps. That meant designing around the locations. Lee found the site of rich husband Sang-woo’s vacation home on a real estate YouTube channel, and the team built the house during two months of pre-production, down to the direction and size of every window. “To create that kind of result requires an enormous amount of calculation, planning and preparation,” Kim said. “Compared to any film I’ve worked on, this is the one where we worried, debated and planned the most to make it appear that way.” Kim’s credits also include effects-heavy productions such as “Ashfall.” “Being human, a certain style inevitably emerges,” he said. “For this project, I wanted to strip those away.” “Possible Love” was shot handheld with a single camera, except for two dialogue scenes. “If it’s too close, it feels exaggerated, and if it’s too far, it feels like we are cropping, cutting up the frame and peeping in,” Kim said of the camera’s distance from the characters. With Ye-ji’s documentary at the heart of the story, separating her footage from Lee’s film was another question. “Is making that distinction really necessary?” Kim said. “So we decided not to set it in stone.” “I wanted to blur that boundary,” he said of the shots from the documentary team’s cameras and his own, which become harder to tell apart as the film goes on. “The reason is hard to explain in words, but it was an intuitive sense that it felt right.” As for the forest, Kim hasn’t given up on the film ghost. “If I get another chance to work with the director in the future, I hope we can definitely meet it then,” he said.
