title: ‘Bedford Park’ Star Moon Choi Charts Her Own Path Between Korea and Hollywood
full_text: × Skip to main content Son Sukku and Moon Choi in ‘Bedford Park.’ Courtesy Indie drama Bedford Park might just prove to be Korean actress Moon Choi’s big break in the U.S. film industry — but she’s nonetheless a little apprehensive about how it will play for the fans who know her work best. “Thinking about the Korean audience, I do get a bit nervous because I don’t know what to expect,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter . After winning an award at Sundance and earning strong reviews in Toronto, Bedford Park is finally meeting Korean moviegoers this week at the Busan International Film Festival — but her fans there will be seeing a rather different side of the star they met in K-dramas like Mistress (2018) or Now, We Are Breaking Up (2021). Related Stories Movies Danny Boyle Shares Why He Used AI for Maggie Thatcher in 'Ink' - Without Asking Her Estate and His Love for 'Obsession' and 'Backrooms' TV The Most Powerful Women in International TV Written and directed by first-time feature filmmaker Stephanie Ahn, Bedford Park stars Choi as Audrey, a 36-year-old Brooklyn physical therapist whose mother’s car accident summons her back to the suburban New Jersey home she has never quite escaped emotionally. The other driver is Eli (rising Korean star Son Sukku of The Roundup and D.P. fame), a prickly former wrestler and Korean adoptee raised by a neglectful white mother. When Audrey visits Eli to share insurance info, the encounter descends into a heated argument over who was responsible for the crash. Their second meeting takes a harrowing turn when Audrey suffers a miscarriage on Eli’s doorstep. Soon, a bond begins to emerge between the two, as they glimpse a kindred spirit hidden beneath each other’s self-defenses. But their intimacy is messy and hard-won, more a meeting of two wounded Asian American survivors and strivers than the typical meet-cute of Korean romances. Choi says she’s uncertain how the story’s milieu of immigrant struggle will resonate with the crowd in Busan, and she suspects “they’re going to be a little bit surprised by just how rated R it is.” Audrey is sexually forthright, self-destructive and resistant to her parents’ preferred version of success, unwilling to become the dutiful daughter they want, even as she feels indebted to their sacrifices. Eli’s fractured family history has left him similarly scarred. But the underlying emotion, Choi believes, should travel. “The film is primarily a family drama and a love story between two people who feel seen for the first time when they meet someone who shares a certain kind of struggle from the past,” she explains. Going into the film’s Sundance premiere, she had wondered whether the characters’ emotional burdens might feel specifically Asian, or unique to immigrant life. But the overwhelmingly positive response from viewers in Park City with neither experience was a gratifying surprise. “I saw so many in the audience crying at the end,” Choi recalls. Busan is also welcoming her as a member of its main competition jury, led by Chinese master Zhang Yimou. For Choi, who has previously judged shorts, the prospect of assessing features alongside such company is both an honor and another exciting challenge ( Bedford Park is screening in the festival’s noncompetitive Flash Forward section). Feeling her way through unfamiliar worlds has been something of a lifelong predicament and opportunity for Choi. Born in Seoul, she moved to Japan at nine, following her father’s banking career. She attended a school in Osaka for ethnic Koreans where lessons were taught in Japanese, later returned to Seoul and eventually moved to New Jersey, where she learned English. Each relocation made her a fresh version of the outsider. “As a kid, I always felt alienated, even when I was back in Korea,” she says. “In Osaka, I tried to fit in with my Japanese friends; back in Seoul, I was viewed as that girl from Japan. In New Jersey, I was trying to learn English and starting all over again.” At around 11, she played the lead in a school production of the classic Korean play The Tale of Sim Cheong and found unexpected relief in the imaginary. “I didn’t have to be Korean. I didn’t have to be Japanese. I just had to play the character,” she remembers. “So I felt very grounded, in a surprising way, and I felt like this was something that I would love to pursue.” She later took acting classes in New Jersey and joined the theater club on her first day of university in Seoul, eventually starring in a series of plays. After an unsuccessful attempt to enter drama school in London, a friend persuaded the self-described theater kid to audition for her first Korean movie. She was thrilled to instantly land a starring role in the girls’ weightlifting drama Lifting King Kong (2009) — but the transition from stage to set was bruising. Accustomed to only winning praise in the theater, Choi says she struggled with the harsh demands of Korean film sets of the time, often going home in tears after her director berated her for failing to deliver the performance he wanted. She also struggled with the unfamiliar aspects of filmmaking. “I didn’t know how to cry on cue; I didn’t know how to block; I didn’t really understand how to perform for a camera,” she says. But rather than retreating to the stage, she decided to seek out short films and independent productions to master the mechanics of movie acting. Her breakthrough came in 2017 with the South Korean biographical period drama Anarchist From Colony , in which she played the real-life Japanese anarchist Kaneko Fumiko. For the first time, the role allowed her to leverage her blended identity and Japanese fluency as a professional asset. The next year, she earned Busan’s actor of the year award for her performance in Korean in Han Ka-ram’s acclaimed drama Our Body . But despite her English abilities, auditioning in Hollywood never occurred to her as a viable possibility — perhaps because so few Korean stars have successfully crossed over to the U.S. industry, she says. That changed in 2019, when her agent, on a whim, sent her Ahn’s screenplay, then titled Audrey Park . Choi usually prints scripts and settles at her desk to read them, but she opened this one on her phone and found herself so engrossed in Audrey’s story that she kept scrolling until the final page. She quickly filmed and sent off some self-tapes but didn’t expect much, assuming the director would have plenty of options among Korean American actors closer to home. Eventually, however, she was invited to New York to audition and landed the role. “When I got the part, I was like, ‘Okay, this is it. This is my debut in Hollywood. I’m going to make it there now too,’” she recalls. Son Suk-ku (L) and Moon Choi (R) arrive on the red carpet during the opening ceremony of the 31st Busan International Film Festival. A few months later, the pandemic hit and the project was derailed as production shut down across the globe. After several years of waiting, Ahn and Choi made a proof-of-concept video to help attract new financing. They filmed the two lead characters’ contentious first encounter, with American actor Clayne Crawford as Eli, who was originally written to be a white guy. Back in Seoul, Choi showed the footage to film industry contacts. Among them was Son, a close friend and frequent stage collaborator whose career was in the process of exploding after his starring parts in the hit drama My Liberation Notes and action blockbuster The Roundup . “This looks good — if the character were a Korean guy, I would love to do it,” she recalls him saying. Choi could instantly picture Son in the role: his physicality, his rough charisma and the familiarity they had developed over multiple stage projects. He had also lived in Chicago and was among the very few major male stars of his generation who spoke fluent English. She proposed to Ahn that Eli become a Korean American adoptee instead. Ahn watched Son’s work, met him over Zoom and agreed. Son’s rising star power then proved vital in unlocking financing. Hyundai Motor Company agreed to back the project, making Bedford Park the automaker’s first investment in an independent feature (the company had previously collaborated with Son on a branded short). By 2025, the cameras were finally rolling, with Choi also serving as an executive producer. The casting shift gave the love story a different cultural dynamic: two people connected to Korea in profoundly different ways, recognizing something in each other that neither could easily explain. For Choi, the project has also become another demonstration of what her own border-crossing background might make possible. Sony Pictures Classics will release Bedford Park in the U.S., with a rollout expected next year. Seoul-based distributor BY4M is planning a wide theatrical run in Korea in February or March. In the meantime, Choi has returned — happily this time — to the theater. In September, she completed the New York run of Simon Stone’s Korean-language adaptation of Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard at the Park Avenue Armory, with pioneering Korean screen icon Jeon Do-yeon playing her mother. For Choi, the play meant performing opposite an actress she has idolized since her youth. Jeon became the first Korean actress to win the Cannes Film Festival’s best actress prize in 2007 for Lee Chang-dong’s Secret Sunshine , and she is now back in the awards conversation with her widely acclaimed performance in the director’s Netflix-backed Oscar contender Possible Love . “She was my hero and my role model. I grew up watching her films. I grew up watching Lee Chang-dong’s films,” Choi says. After three years collaborating on international stagings of the play, Jeon offered some encouragement that Choi says she is still absorbing. On their final night, the veteran took her hand and urged her to recognize and embrace her own abilities — and to chase the rare opportunity that her unique background has opened up. “The gist of it is that she told me to pursue this path that no one has ever walked before as a Korean actress, because I’m multilingual. That made me really emotional,” Choi says. “Saying it still makes me emotional right now.” Choi now plans to audition in the U.S. while continuing to pursue projects in Korea, where she has another play scheduled for the spring. The goal is not to abandon one home for another, but to explore whether a balance between two industry bases is possible. “For now, my focus is to find a powerful story like Bedford Park in the U.S. or Korea, whether it be a film or TV series or any kind of medium,” she says. “I don’t know what to expect. But I am open to this new journey.” THR

title: BlumFest Haunts New York Comic Con 2026: All the Highlights From Blumhouse Atomic Monster
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All October 9, 2026 6:14pm Jason Blum, Curry Barker and Cooper Tomlinson speak at BlumFest 2026 during New York Comic Con 2026 at Javits Center on October 09, 2026 in New York City. Craig Barritt/Getty Images for ReedPop Logo text BlumFest revealed Craig Zobel as the director for the adaptation of James Tynion IV and Werther Dell’Edera’s Something is Killing the Children, while also debuting the trailer for The Exorcist: Martyrs , and teasing upcoming projects including Seasons , RoboCop , Molepeople, and more. The two-hour Friday night panel featured an A-List lineup, including Mike Flanagan, James Wan, Chiwetel Ejiofor, David Harbour , LaKeith Stanfield, Curry Barker , and Kristen Bell . About halfway through the panel, the entire 2027 lineup was revealed, including River (Jan. 15), The Revenge of Llorona (Feb. 26), The Exorcist: Martyrs , Anything but Ghosts (May 7), Paranormal Activity (May 21), The Blair Witch Project (Sept. 24) and Sleepover and Seasons (Nov. 12). The list also included a currently untitled film set for August 2027. Related Stories Movies LaKeith Stanfield, Ben Mendelsohn to Star in 'Molepeople' for Atomic Monster, Paramount Primal (Exclusive) TV 'Crystal Lake' Will Offer More Brutal Kills Than Films, Go Deep on Jason's Background During a panel, which served as a victory lap for Blumhouse Atomic Monster ’s box office hits Backrooms and Obsession , producer and Blumhouse co-founder Jason Blum teased what is ahead for the studio. “It’s been an incredible year, and what’s so cool about the movies you listed is how different they all are. Everybody has a different idea about what’s scary, and that is what I love about horror ,” he said. “We want to work with filmmakers who never stop surprising you. And a year like we’ve had, with the help of movies like Obsession , gives us more opportunity to take more chances, and you’ll get a taste of those chances and risks and weird stuff tonight.” Earlier in the day, IDW Dark and Blumhouse announced they were teaming on a Happy Death Day comic series from Blumhouse and IDW Dark, with writer Tim Seeley ( Hack/Slash ) attached to translate the time-loop slasher and expand its mystery ahead of a third movie. Read below for more on what was unveiled during BlumFest 2026 at New York Comic Con. Anything But Ghosts Towards the end of the panel, Barker and Cooper Tomlinson were brought out on stage, and briefly discussed how his life had changed in just a year. After reflecting on Obsession and the nature of their partnership, the duo teased Anything But Ghosts , which follows ghost hunter con artists who “get a huge job, a bigger one than they’ve ever gotten before. But it’s a real ghost, so they have to step up and be the thing that they promised.” The film will see Barker co-star with Tomlinson. “I need him on camera with me. We wrote this together thinking this will be the movie that we starred in together, an homage to what we’ve been doing online,” Barker said. “I didn’t write Obsession with me necessarily in mind, but we knew we had to do these two characters.” Barker also expressed that the film will take a similar approach to their work on Obsession , trying to subvert horror film tropes and expectations. “I think, just me as an audience member who’s been watching horror movies my entire life, you can take the blueprint of a horror movie, and know what audiences are expecting. You can actually use that to your advantage to say, if I’m an audience member and I’m watching this and I know what’s going to happen next, how can I subvert that? You can expect that same attitude as Anything But Ghosts .” Amanda the Adventurer Among the new partnerships announced at the panel was a deal with Matthew Patrick, aka MatPat, the founder and former host of the “Theory” Channels on YouTube. Patrick will work with the studio to develop new films based on indie games and horror channels to bring those stories to the big screen. “We are giving them the spotlight they deserve,” Patrick said during the panel. The first announced project is a feature film based on DreadXP’s indie video game Amanda the Adventurer . A teaser at the panel also previewed footage of the online horror phenomenon, a series of clips that combines the animated children’s show-esque story with unsettling interstitials. “We are currently in talks with writers and directors, so more is coming soon. We’re moving really fast on that one,” Patrick said. Molepeople & Seasons Among the newer projects is RoboCop , which Wan noted is currently being developed as a series for Amazon Prime with the original writer Edward Neumeier and Dan Stevens in the titular role. The second major project out of the studio is Rob Savage’s next Blumhouse Atomic Monster film Molepeople , starring Lakeith Stanfield , his return to the studio following the game-changing Get Out . Described by Savage “as a subterranean horror movie that’s going to scare the living shit out of you,” the film will be in the vein of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre and The Hills Have Eyes , with Savage noting the movie will begin filming very soon. Speaking to the connections between Get Out and Molepeople , Stanfield shared that the 2018 Jordan Peele film “was fantastical on the outside, but there was some heart in it on the inside, and I think that’s the kind of thing I like to replicate and continue to have in my career.” He added, “I found something that I think can be engaging, action-packed, cool, fun, and also a little bit of commentary, too.” Wan also teased a new movie with Companion director Drew Hancock, Seasons , which is based on the “No Sleep” subreddit story. “It’s a horror movie that takes place over four seasons,” the producer told the audience after a video featuring Hancock on set with Ron Perlman. Additional titles teased included The Blair Witch Project , with Dylan Clark set to helm, and a new Paranormal Activity entry from Undertones director Ian Tuason, with a video from the director hyping the entry. “ Paranormal Activity is such an emotional movie for me because it’s really how Blumhouse started, and it really gave birth to everything that we’ve done,” said Blum. “I hate the idea that you keep making movies and then drive it into the ground, so we stopped making them for a long time. What got me excited is that my partner, who, in my humble opinion, has created three of the greatest horror franchises of all time, which no one else has ever done, came to me.” Added the producer: “For me, it was enough to hear that, and that’s really what made it happen. People ask me how do you choose what movies go to Blumhouse or Atomic Monster? It’s a very simple answer. Whatever James doesn’t want, we do.” Wan also spoke about returning to the Saw universe, telling the NYCC crowd that going with director Mike P. Nelson was about “his sensibility” and how he “really prioritizes surprises in his movies. I think the Saw movies are full of surprises, right? It’s all twists and turns. It’s not just about the traps. It’s about the moral dilemma. It’s about the visual style.” Something Is Killing the Children As part of the final portion of the jam-packed panel, Something Is Killing the Children creator James Dickinson, as well as the newly announced director Noel, appeared on stage to tease their upcoming title. “My first conversation with Jason about this was really incredible. We have been building the world on Instagram for about seven years now, and we’ve now reached over five million readers around the world. But we’ve always known that this is a franchise that had the potential to reach a much, much bigger audience,” Dickinson said. The duo was pretty mum on when production would start or any filming locations but they did briefly tease what they’re excited about with the characters. While Dickinson confirmed fans can expect to see Octo — the story’s stuffed Octopus with a monster trapped inside it — Noel is quite excited for how fans will experience the story’s protagonist, Erica Slaughter. The director described her as “such a powerful badass” and not only strong, but able to “lift axes and dismember 15-foot monsters,” which the film will get to illustrate. “We also see how funny she can be and that Erica, in the midst of something killing the children, has this very bone-dry humor we’ve really got to nail.” Dickinson also confirmed there would be children killed onscreen. “The first time that Jason and I talked about it, about 20 to 30 minutes into the conversation, I was like, ‘You’ve, like, read the copy? This would be intense,’” he recalled. “It’s called Something Is Killing the Children , and, you know, I promise you, there are kids who die.” Violent Night 2 Violent Night stars David Harbour and Kristen Bell were also joined on stage by director Tommy Wirkola and producer Kelly McCormick. While discussing his return to an unusual role, Harbour shared that the sequel happened because there’s “a lot of really rabid, crazy fans out there, and they wanted to know more about Santa’s backstory specifically, and how he got those tattoos and lots of different things. I would go to cons like this, and people would bring up all these questions, and I would video them, and I would send them to Kelly and Tommy. They wrote a script, and it’s really exciting to bring you guys some more Santa.” Bell, who joins the sequel as Mrs. Klaus, shared she was “so confused” she got the call for the role, as she wasn’t aware of a second film. But says her character, “Mrs. Klaus is substantially older than Mr. Klaus. Take that how you will, but if you’re looking at the lore of who came first — and I know the first one, there were sort of moments where you saw his Viking mythology v you’ll get a taste of what Mrs. Klaus’ elven history is.” The section featured several clips, including an intense multi-minute fight sequence where Harbour’s Santa takes on some henchmen with the tools of a bakery, ending in someone getting cooked, literally. Another clip teased a few more sequences in a moment from the trailer, which sees Bell’s Mrs. Klaus arrive to save the day. Speaking to how she prepared for the role, Bell shared that she had a stunt double, but also trained for five weeks ahead of filming. “It was some of the most fun I had ever had at 87North working with stunt people who know exactly what they’re doing and are teaching me about my body and how I can move. I had always known that the physicality of the character is really important, just as important as the words you’re saying,” she said. “Do you take up space in a room, or do you sit back? Are you imposing? What you’re doing with your body can really tell a story. I feel like a billion bucks having learned this choreo.” “It’s basically Miracle on 34th Street with an enormous bloody hammer,” teased Harbour, later revealing, alongside the film’s director, that the original film and its sequel are influenced by Home Alone and Die Hard , which will get its own vent nod in Violent Night 2 . The Exorcist: Martyrs As part of a brief panel that revealed the first trailer for the film, out March 12, Flanagan and Ejiofor teased a movie that is “so god damn scary.” “I can feel it on set. It was freaking me out in my chair,” Flanagan said. “This movie is unlike any other Exorcist movie that’s ever been made, which was something that we were really determined, all of us, to do from the very beginning. It was to take this franchise in a completely different direction. One of the things that we all agreed on going in was that it had to be scary.” Speaking to expanding the larger Exorcist universe, Flannigan shared that, “I’ve been lucky enough or crazy enough in my career now several times to step into a franchise underneath a monolithic titan of the genre and have to carry that torch a little further.” He continued: “It is really intimidating because The Exorcist is The Exorcist , and it’s not just [William] Friedkin’s masterpiece that we’re stepping into the shadow of. It’s an entire franchise that has struck out in different directions every time they come to bat. It’s like, they’re going this way, they’re going that way. You’re seeing all sorts of different expressions of this central idea — and it wasn’t just The Exorcist . We talked an awful lot about The Exorcist III , for example. I think [it’s] one of the most underrated, underappreciated films in the franchise. The hallway scene, iconic.” For Ejiofor, the terror is partly in the feeling. “I think with these, with the way that it talks about that feeling, how do you describe it? That feeling that’s sort of there that you feel can sometimes be a force, a malevolent force that’s just around. Sometimes you can put a name to it. Sometimes you can’t, but you can just sort of feel it around you. And with this, it really felt like it was entering.” River Following a video message from writer-director Joshua Giuliano, who introduced the film’s trailer but wasn’t present because he is currently prepping his next Blumhouse film Occupant in Vancouver, star of the film Jessica Rothe came to tease the river thriller. Also starring Jane Levy, Max Mattern, and Dane DiLiegro, the film is “wild,” but also a family drama, with “heartfelt moments, terror, a psychotic six-foot-eight ripped, super hot but very scary man,” according to the actress. Speaking to the demands of filming a movie so heavily based in water, she told the NYCC crowd that 14 of the 22 shoot days were on the water. “It’s such a gift as an actor to be able to be in the physical element that you’re actually supposed to be in. Because the fear you see on my face when Dane, our incredible masked man, is swimming after me, that’s real fear because I was like, that man is going to catch me. He is definitely faster than I am, and it just adds another element of reality and terror and fun.” Horror Short With Creator Heidi Wong Blumhouse Atomic Monster also announced a new short film development deal with multimedia horror storyteller and content creator Heidi Wong. Known as “The Horror Queen,” Wong will create a new horror short film for Blumhouse Atomic Monster through her new development deal. Speaking to tapping creators, Blum noted that what “Kane [Pareons] did and what Curry did, original voices and a fresh point of view and a new take on something we haven’t seen before, is more effective in the world than it’s ever been, which is exciting. It’s exciting for me. It’s much more fun to do what I do. It’s more fun to watch what we all watch, as a result of that. As we continue going forward, we’re always trying to find new, different, original ways to scare all of you and all of us.” While speaking about the deal on stage with Wong, Blum noted that they are looking to “develop, and hopefully make [the short] into a future film.” While Wong was pretty mum about the plot, she noted her butterfly dress and social media easter eggs hinted at the short’s focus. “It’s inspired by Eastern mythology and folklore,” she told the crowd. “I grew up in Asia, so it’s very close to me, and to have Blumhouse’s support really means so much.” THR

title: ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay Delivers Another Essential and Compelling Constitutional Deep Dive for Netflix
full_text: Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All October 9, 2026 6:00pm Ava DuVernay and Dr. Carla Hayden in '14th' Netflix Logo text On November 3, U.S. voters will cast ballots in midterm elections that will go a long way toward shaping or reshaping our government. The results will offer a pivotal snapshot of how the country is currently viewing the solvency of our particular brand of democracy. Ava DuVernay ‘s new documentary for Netflix focuses on the 14th Amendment to the Constitution, recent attempts to strip the 14th Amendment of its power, and the ways in which the 14th Amendment embodies and represents the ideals and long-term viability of the American experiment. Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Returns With One of Netflix's Most Political Docs Ever: "This Movie Kicked My Butt" Movies Now It's Clear Why Amazon Didn't Want to Release 'Artificial': It's Withering AF 14th The Bottom Line Infuriating and inspiring in the right ways. Venue: New York Film Festival (Closing Night) Release date: November 27 (theatrical); December 4 (Netflix) Director: Ava DuVernay 1 hour 48 minutes Naturally, Netflix has set 14th for a brief theatrical run on November 27 ahead of a streaming premiere on December 4th. A sequel or companion to DuVernay’s Oscar-nominated 13th , the doc is a cogent, urgent clarion call, and Netflix is sending it straight to the scheduling equivalent of voicemail. I’m baffled, but I guess it isn’t my job to review programming choices or corporate politics. Like its predecessor — I briefly was outraged recalling that 13th lost the Oscar, until I was reminded that OJ: Made in America won — 14th is powered by well-earned rage; also like its predecessor, it’s more a history lesson and a model of carefully composed rhetoric than a screed. As anybody who studied Constitutional amendments in school — and why isn’t that everybody? — knows, there are plenty of amendments that can be summed up in a catchy phrase: “Alcohol? No!” “Actually, alcohol? Sure!” “Vote at 18!” “Vote if you’re a woman!” “Cruel and unusual punishment, like when a state is unable to correctly administer the death penalty (or, actually, the death penalty itself)? No!” Etc., etc. DuVernay’s last documentary focused on the supposed simplicity of the 13th Amendment, which outlawed slavery and involuntary servitude, except in cases where the prison industrial complex is involved. It’s a simple amendment, but the hypocrisy around its implementation remains complicated. The 14th Amendment is not one of the simple ones. As Stacey Abrams, part of a wide-ranging group of talking heads here, puts it, the 14th Amendment is the “everything bagel” of constitutional amendments. As Dr. Eric Foner puts it, the 14th Amendment is the most important since the Bill of Rights. As Dr. Sherrilyn Ifill explains in some depth, the 13th, 14th and 15th amendments reflect a grand reimagining of the American experiment in the aftermath of the Civil War — almost a second Constitution. The amendment offers a new definition for citizenship, one built on equality, particularly in issues of due process and equal protection under the law. It’s the foundation for Supreme Court decisions allowing for interracial and gay marriage, the origin of birthright citizenship, and the reason why paying off the January 6th insurrectionists is blatantly unconstitutional. It is, in modern TV and movie terms, a constitutional reboot, and like so many reboots, it has sparked debate about what is and isn’t canonical to the intention of its framers — both the original constitutional framers and the framers of these bridge amendments, including John Bingham, Thaddeus Stevens and Charles Sumner. Note that the documentary promises to remove the obscurity around this second group of framers and, unfortunately, it doesn’t come close. DuVernay and her various talking heads establish quickly why the 14th Amendment is so essential, and then go into depth on the attempts to erase the amendment’s protections over the years, with a particular focus on the decades of efforts to erase the immediate gains of Reconstruction. Some of that will be familiar to regular viewers of documentary and comedy/news programs, especially when it comes to the evisceration of the Daughters of the Confederacy, the perpetuation of the Lost Cause myth, and the erection of countless monuments to the various slaveholders and insurrectionists who fought for the South. I attended a Jefferson Davis Elementary School in my youth — since renamed for Barack Obama — so much of this hit hard and close to home. In addition to the usual historians, constitutional scholars, populist commentators and politicians — including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Jasmine Crockett, Alex Padilla and dedicated regurgitator of MAGA talking points Anna Paulina Luna — DuVernay weaves in ground-level vignettes. We spend time with the likes of Devon Henry, the contractor tasked with removing Richmond’s Confederate monuments, and Dr. Carla Hayden, fired as the Librarian of Congress for poorly articulated reasons related to the current administration’s war on DEI. The documentary is fairly straightforward, but never visually dull. DuVernay stages her interviews in a diverse assortment of settings, moving the camera in a way that’s kinetic but never nauseating. There’s a frequently utilized effect that brings to life vintage black-and-white photos, which comes across as an extension of Ken Burns’ beloved technique with a computer-effects twist that I don’t fully understand, but it keeps things lively. The argument DuVernay builds is deftly constructed within the 108 minutes of the documentary, escalating from past to present to future and from dryly historical to emotional and visceral. Spencer Averick’s editing and the score by Jason Moran retain a high intensity throughout, evoking a heist movie in which the main antagonists are out to steal your rights. Which is apt, I guess. The documentary generates anger, sadness and even, by showcasing clips from the likes of George Carlin and Hasan Minhaj, humor. More than that, though, 14th made me wish for two things: First, that DuVernay continue her amendment-by-amendment documentary series until we eventually get her exposé on the timetable of Congressional salary increases. Second, that given the effort DuVernay puts into these films, it would be nice if they were released at the time when they could most successfully stir people to action. Full credits Venue: New York Film Festival (Closing Night) Distributor: Netflix Production Company: Array Filmworks in association with Array Alliance Director: Ava DuVernay Producers: Ava DuVernay, Spencer Averick, Tammy Garnes, Paul Garnes Editor: Spencer Averick Cinematographers: Michael Cambio Fernandez, Clifford Charles Composer: Jason Moran 1 hour 48 minutes THR

title: Roseanne Barr’s Self-Produced TV Series Now Courting Distributors, Co-Creator Says
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All October 9, 2026 5:09pm Roseanne Barr Araya Doheny/Getty Images Roseanne Barr ’s new independently produced television series is being shopped to distributors and has fielded interest from a few, according to her co-creator on the project. “We have a lot of nibbles right now,” writer-producer Allan Stephan told The Hollywood Reporter on Friday. Representatives for the comedy series, co-created by Stephan and Barr and called Meemaw : A Modern-Day Fable , have been sending a trailer around to interested parties and targeting streamers. Stephan didn‘t name any specific platforms that have been sniffing around but said “I know [representatives for the show] are in talks with a few places.” (Of course, as the co-creator of the series, Stephan has a vested interest in portraying the project as in-demand.) Page Six Hollywood broke the news on Thursday that the former sitcom star, whose Roseanne reboot on ABC was canceled in 2018 after Barr posted an offensive tweet about former advisor to President Barack Obama Valerie Jarrett, had filmed the eight-episode indie series. Meemaw is said to follow the matriarch (played by Barr) of a Texas family of preppers who is attempting to organize a blowout bat mitvah for her granddaughter. Alongside Barr, Randy Quaid, Drea de Matteo, Omar Gooding, Doug Jones and Indy Bugg star. Comedians Jon Lovitz, Tony Hinchcliffe and Kim Congdon make cameos in the series, which shot in Austin. Comedy scribe and producer Allen Covert ( Murder Mystery, Eight Crazy Nights ), a longtime collaborator of Adam Sandler, helped write the series. “They’re struggling farmers, where everybody is at today, especially farmers,“ Stephan said of the show’s characters. “And it’s about surviving in the world as it is today, trying to keep food in the table and the family together.“ None of this guarantees Meemaw is coming to a major streaming platform. Plenty of creators of independent shows engage in talks with companies and not all of them land a deal. But it does appear to show that, eight years after her eponymous show‘s cancellation at ABC, Barr isn’t a total pariah in Hollywood. Barr raised the money independently for Meemaw’ s first season with the help of her son, Jake Pentland, Stephan said. He added that he didn’t know the details of the fundraising efforts, leaving the question of which funders wanted to help bring a new Barr project to the world unanswered for now. ( THR has reached out to Pentland for comment.) The episodes of Meemaw are 30 minutes each, but don‘t call it a sitcom. “We call it a fable because part of the storytelling involves some animals and it’s just a little different,” Stephan said. After breaking into entertainment as a stand-up comic, Barr shot to stardom in the late ’80s with her ABC sitcom Roseanne , where she played a working-class mom in Illinois. After concluding in 1997, the show was rebooted in 2018 at ABC until Barr‘s tweet led to its cancellation. Barr apologized at the time for the tweet saying, “I apologize to Valerie Jarrett and to all Americans. I am truly sorry for making a bad joke about her politics and her looks. I should have known better. Forgive me — my joke was in bad taste.” Stephan says Barr‘s latest project is a nonpartisan effort meant to appeal to the masses, much like Roseanne did in its heyday. “The show is very representative of all people,” he said. “There’s no Trump side, there’s no democratic side. It’s just the family struggling to get by and what they have to deal with to get by.” THR

title: Israeli Americans Protest ‘NAZA’ Los Angeles Screening as Doc Releases Theatrically in U.S.

Israeli-American Council (IAC) During a Friday screening of NAZA at Laemmle NoHo 7 in North Hollywood, dozens of Israeli-Americans and members of the Jewish community protested outside the theater. The documentary is from Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who previously said in a statement that they “made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible.” Some protestors were wrapped in Israeli and American flags, holding signs that read, “Learn the Facts. Know the Truth.” and “Movies Have Editors. History Does Not.” Images documenting the Oct. 7 attack were also shown, alongside posters calling for the return of hostages. Related Stories Movies Swiss Queer Film Fest Drops Israeli Film After Boycott Threats: "We're Not Sundance, Right?" Movies For Israeli Actress Noa Cohen, October 7 Is Both Personal and Professional “Our message is clear: wherever lies are told about Israel , we will show up with the truth,” said Aya Shechter, the Israeli-American Council (IAC)’s chief operating officer in a statement. “Everyone who came out today is saying, loudly and clearly, that we stand with Israel. Especially around October 7, we do not forget those who were murdered and those who fell, and we are standing here also for those who can no longer stand here to shout the truth themselves.” The September premiere of NAZA at the New York Film Festival was also met with protestors organized by the IAC. Nova festival survivors Rom El-Hai and Shalev Biton were among those who spoke. “We’re here not because we’re saying, don’t show the film,” IAC co-chair Tal Shuster said of NAZA during the New York rally. “Everyone has the freedom of speech, that’s the United States. We are saying: it’s not all the facts. Show everything else, not just the documentary.” “We have the trucks here,” Shuster continued. “Let’s each one of us be an ambassador and show people what actually happened. If you screen the film, invite a survivor, let them speak, at a panel. Let them be heard. Don’t just show one side without the facts from the other side. Before you go into the film, or after it, come hear about what happened in Israel on Oct. 7. 1,200 people were murdered. 251 people were kidnapped. Yes, show all the facts.” At the Venice Film Festival, NAZA received the Special Jury Prize . The doc released theatrically in the United States on Friday. THR

title: Lisa and Director Sue Kim on Documenting the Star’s Break From the K-pop System in ‘Always Lalisa’
full_text: × Skip to main content The global pop star gives a shockingly honest look into her journey breaking out of the K-pop system as a solo artist. Courtesy of Sony Music Vision Was it fate that sent Lisa into the global spotlight? Always Lalisa , Sue Kim’s documentary on the global superstar, starts with the K-pop idol-turned-actress and her mother recounting her visit to a fortune teller that ended with a suggestion to change her daughter’s name to Lalisa. It would be a name loved by many, the fortune teller told her mother. Lisa, whose real name is Lalisa Manobal, remembers the change well. “I think I was 13,” the singer tells The Hollywood Reporter . It’s been a whirlwind year since the cameras stopped rolling for Always Lalisa , which chronicles the singer’s year away from the record-breaking girl group Blackpink . Related Stories Movies George Clooney Explains Why The Albies Shine a Light on Justice: "It Feels Like It's in Short Supply" Music Lola Young, Muna, Tinashe Join Lineup for Chappell Roan's Super Graphic Spectacular Benefit Shows The pop star explains in the documentary that she and the rest of Blackpink — Jennie, Jisoo and Rosé — promised each other that they’d take a year away from the group to pursue solo endeavors. Throughout that year away, Lisa released her first full-length album, Alter Ego , starred in The White Lotus and snagged herself a Coachella solo lineup spot. Lisa was brought up in the busy world of K-pop, consistently heading from one appearance to another as a member of Blackpink. But the documentary shows the star even more committed to packing every moment she can into her schedule. It was nonstop, but it wasn’t exactly the same. “It felt different,” she says. “At first, that one-year break wasn’t the plan — that I was going to squeeze in everything. More or less, we just wanted to take a break and find the things that we wanted to do,” she says. “At first, [I thought] maybe I’m going to travel. But The White Lotus opportunity came in and I didn’t want to waste that one-year time.” Last summer, she and Blackpink reunited after their year apart to record another group EP, Deadline , released in February, and headed out on a world tour. Now the women of the group are back to releasing solo music again — Lisa recently performed her single “SaWaDiKa” at the the MTV Video Music Awards, where she took home the best pop award — and her schedule is similar to what it was in that year “break.” Lalisa Manobal at the premiere of ‘Always Lalisa’ during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Robin Marchant/Getty Images The doc showcases Lisa’s family and friends from her home country of Thailand in a way that her time as a K-pop star didn’t often afford her. K-pop has historically been an industry that holds idols — the name given to pop stars in the Korean entertainment industry — to an extremely high standard. Their personal lives are often showcased in a way that’s entirely filtered through the entertainment company’s lens. Kim wasn’t looking to do that. “I knew from the get go that I was operating under different instructions, that I was going to be able to work with a beloved K-pop idol away from the K-pop system,” the director says. “That was so appealing to me because that meant, ‘Oh, I can approach this honestly and I can approach it with intimacy and vulnerability and truth about what their lives are like.'” In one of the most honest moments of the film, Lisa admits that, like many young women her age, she wants to get married and have children. But there is a lingering concern that her fans won’t like that. “I hope they understand me more,” Lisa says when asked about the vulnerable moment from the film. “I’m just a girl, we want the same thing at the end of the day. That’s it. I just want them to understand me more.” Blackpink appears throughout the film, but it focues mostly on Lisa’s life outside the group. Kim’s intention was to make sure it didn’t feel like a K-pop film. “It was a film about someone who had achieved a great amount of success in a K-pop girl group, but we were covering her year away from that, kind of discovering herself and figuring out a new path for her solo career,” she says. Kim naturally had to bring in Lisa’s past to explain how she got to this point, but she purposefully kept it limited. Part of that was a creative choice, but the director also wanted to incorporate more of Blackpink’s songs and music videos, particularly from the trainee years, so audiences could hear what Lisa sounded like as a member of the group. Ultimately, it didn’t work out logistically. Lisa performs at the 2025 Coachella Valley Music And Arts Festival. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images for Coachella “Despite our best efforts, we were not allowed to license the music or the footage, so that was it,” Kim says. “That was our only interaction with her previous label and the small amount of the K-pop lore that I wanted to bring into it, we weren’t able to.” The film does take on one uncomfortable piece of that history, however: a recent controversy surrounding leaked trainee videos of Lisa and some of the Blackpink members singing songs with the N-word. The singer had previously been silent on the matter, as it’s revealed in the documentary, that appears to be a mix of the K-pop label’s suggestion and death threats aimed at her. She is apologetic in the film. “I feel like I didn’t have a chance to really say [an apology],” she says. “Through this documentary, I wanted to share that.” The director clarifies that the moment came up organically in filming. “We obviously get her in a very unguarded moment talking about what was happening on the couch,” she says, speaking to the scene where the singer reacts to the leaked videos. “That was the day that the videos were released.” It was not, Kim emphasizes, a scripted moment. “That wasn’t her deciding she wanted to say something. That was literally us in the moment with her while she’s dealing with this shocking thing that happened,” the director says. “You can see it in her reaction and that conversation, you can really feel the emotions. She’s sad and she’s disappointed in herself and she’s regretful.” The documentary ends with Lisa’s return to Korea to begin preparations for Blackpink’s world tour and the group’s latest album. On screen, she seems nervous to return to the previous version of herself. “We’re human. We have fear,” she says now. “I feel like we learned so much during the break,” she continues. “When we go back [now], it’s even better. Everybody comes back with an amazing energy. We miss each other so much, and we’re like, ‘OK, we’re locked in. We’re back, guys.'” Lisa’s now focused on her latest single “SaWaDiKa” and her upcoming EP Press Play , due Oct. 23. “I’m so happy that [the fans] can finally hear it because I’ve been keeping this to myself for some time,” she says of her latest single. She’ll perform the song, and many more, at her upcoming Las Vegas residency. Watching that year back through the documentary has only strengthened Lisa’s belief in herself. “Truly that’s real me,” she says. “What I’ve gone through, how hard that I worked.” “I’m just so proud of myself,” she adds. Always Lalisa is in theaters for a limited time beginning Oct. 12. THR
